speakeroldname: Mr. W. L. M. Creaghan (Westmorland) moved

speechtext: for leave to introduce a bill to amend the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act (to include provident fund pensioners).

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO INCLUDE PROVIDENT FUND PENSIONERS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO INCLUDE PROVIDENT FUND PENSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the provident fund act was passed in 1907 to permit public servants employed by government owned and operated railways to contribute to a pension plan. The fund is administered by a board of five directors, one of whom is the
2280	HOUSE OF
Public Service Pension Adjustment Act regional manager of the C.N.R., two are appointed by the Minister of Transport and two are elected annually by the employees. The secretary is appointed by order in council. The board meets regularly at the fund's headquarters in Moncton.
As of the end of 1958 provident fund pensions were paid by Department of Transport cheques to 4,013 retired employees, and at that date there were still 1,941 employees in active service and contributing to the fund. The figures are smaller today. The fund is subsidized by the Canadian National and by annual vote of the Department of Transport. This year's vote is No. 120 under the heading pensions-railway employees provident fund.
The existing legislation appears to include provident fund pensioners. This amendment will simply clarify the point and make certain that those retired public servants can come under the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act passed in this house in 1959.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO INCLUDE PROVIDENT FUND PENSIONERS
speechtext: Before placing this motion before the house I wonder whether the hon. member who proposes it could satisfy the house that the bill does not involve the expenditure of public funds. It appears on its face, if it is effective, to extend the number of ex-employees who would secure benefits under the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act, and certainly those adjusted benefits involve the expenditure of public funds. Without saying more than that, perhaps the hon. member has thought about this question and may have the answer to the difficulty I feel is inherent in the bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO INCLUDE PROVIDENT FUND PENSIONERS
speechtext:
I have given some consideration to this technicality. It seems to me that the resolution introduced in 1959 by the Minister of Finance, and the legislation passed, were broad enough to include this group of public servants. The schedule to the act, paragraph 10, contains the same words as are in the explanatory notes to my bill that the adjustment could be paid to people who in the opinion of treasury board were in receipt of pension "calculated on the basis of length of service".
I believe that the legislation already passed is broad enough to include this group, but I have ascertained that treasury board has not seen fit to so include them. When I voted for the bill in 1959 I thought the provident fund pensioners were included. As Your Honour will recall, it includes members of the armed forces, retired federal civil servants and members of the R.C.M.P. who, like provident fund pensioners prior to 1922 when the C.N.R. came into existence, were contributing to a government pension or superannuation.

I feel I am not asking this parliament to vote money. I want the previous legislation clarified and, second, I would point out that the bill I am introducing today does not say that parliament shall vote the funds. It simply says "if in the opinion of treasury board," which means parliament will not be deciding, but treasury board will.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO INCLUDE PROVIDENT FUND PENSIONERS
speechtext: Abrogation of responsibility.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF LEGISLATION TO INCLUDE PROVIDENT FUND PENSIONERS

maintopic: PUBLICITY GIVEN TO NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING SKILLED WORKERS
speechtext:
I
wish to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. In view of newspaper reports that little publicity is being given to the relaxed admission requirements for skilled immigrants, would the minister inform the house what action she is taking to ensure that people are informed of, and understand, the latest regulations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: PUBLICITY GIVEN TO NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING SKILLED WORKERS
speechtext:
I saw the article referred to in this morning's press, and I should like to say that there is no truth whatever in the suggestion that the immigration department is deliberately holding back on publicizing the recent changes in the immigration regulations, as was said in that article.
When the changes were announced in the house on January 19 last, full publicity was given to them in the press and through the news media both in Canada and overseas. Copies of the new regulations and information pertaining to them were distributed immediately to the ethnic press in Canada. There has been wide editorial and news comment on the new regulations.
In addition we have supplied all our immigration offices overseas, all our Canadian diplomatic missions abroad, and British consular authorities who act for us in other places with full information in respect of the new regulations and how we expect them to operate. This information is available to any and all who may be interested. We have provided information through established diplomatic channels here in Ottawa to all governments which have expressed an interest. We have supplemented the written information with discussions in a good many instances with representatives of India, Pakistan, Ceylon and Japan, to give but a few examples.
We have not, of course, inserted paid advertisements in the press overseas or gone on radio or television in foreign countries. That has never been the policy of the government or of the department. Moreover, many overseas governments exercise very firm control over the types and amounts of publicity relating to immigration which they will permit within their jurisdictions. But it is nonsense to suggest that publicity relating to the new regulations is being deliberately held back.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

maintopic: PUBLICITY GIVEN TO NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING SKILLED WORKERS
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask a supplementary question. Can the hon. lady say whether there has been any increase in the staff of any of the immigration offices in order to deal with the additional applicants resulting from the less stringent regulations, and whether any new offices have been opened anywhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
maintopic: PUBLICITY GIVEN TO NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING SKILLED WORKERS
speechtext:
The answer to that question is no. During consideration of the estimates last year, I think, someone asked me whether we had decreased the overseas staff. The answer to that question was no. We expect that the existing staff will be adequate to handle the increased flow. However, we do anticipate that there may be additional countries to which it will be necessary to supply staff, possibly, in the first instance, in the form of travelling teams. The hon. member is familiar with that procedure. If there is sufficient flow from any country to warrant the opening of an office, that may well have to be considered as the need arises.
Although I told the hon. member yesterday that it was as yet too early to expect any actual entries into Canada, I might say that the increase in interest abroad and in applications from abroad has been pronounced since February 1.

maintopic: PUBLICITY GIVEN TO NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING SKILLED WORKERS
speechtext: Perhaps I might be permitted to ask the hon. lady another supplementary question. Can she say whether the department has sent any officials to the British West Indies, or whether such action is contemplated?

maintopic: PUBLICITY GIVEN TO NEW REGULATIONS RESPECTING SKILLED WORKERS
speechtext: When any decisions are made along those lines they will be announced.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned yesterday, I was saying that the government resorted to all possible publicity

to praise certain measures it had implemented. Now, I shall tell you about the pitiful situation of the dairy industry.
There are 350,000 dairy farmers in Canada and 100,000 in the province of Quebec alone. That is why, of course, I made those few remarks yesterday and I should like to proceed along that line today.
While in 1957, every Canadian consumed an average of 1,021 pounds of dairy products, that figure fell to 940 pounds in 1960, and there is every indication that the consumption of those products is still decreasing.
Three years ago, Canada was the fourth highest consumer of dairy products in the world and it was only the sixth in 1960.
If you refer to La Presse of February 21, 1962, under the heading "Lowest farm income since 1957", you can read the following:
Net farm Income, In 1961, including changes in stocks of grain and livestock, amounted to some $1,006 million, a decrease of 24 per cent from the adjusted estimate of 1960 ($1,319,600,000) and the lowest income since 1957 ($1,058,300,000).

As for his record, he should not forget that the capsule holding the American cosmonaut has been recovered, while his own not only has not been recovered but is not recoverable, and it will land in opposition on election night.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take advantage of this item, departmental administration, to deal very briefly with the policy of the party we represent in respect of agriculture. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance is looking askance at me, but I am quite in order and I shall be as brief as possible.
Everyone here who thinks at all about the development of our economy gives some consideration to the necessity for planning, whether it is in the field of agriculture, in the field of industry or in other aspects of

our economy, and recognizes that major planning must take place. Some want this planning under the auspices of the large corporations, others want it under government auspices, and others want it from other directions. However, I believe this principle is generally accepted in our modern society.
There are different approaches toward planning. I would say that in so far as planning for agriculture is concerned-I intend to use agricultural terms-the attitude of the Progressive Conservatives is one of somewhat laying back on the breeching; so far as the Liberals are concerned I would say they are pawing the ground, and so far as the New Democratic party is concerned I would say they are leaning forward and straining in the collar. In case some of our suburbanite representatives do not understand that language and are not acquainted with horses, possibly I should put it in other terms. I should say that members on the government side are inclined to have their foot on the brake; members of the official opposition have their feet on the floor, and members of the New Democratic party are stepping on the accelerator. I think in general that fairly describes the approach toward planning of the various groups in this house, and toward agricultural planning in particular.
If I might digress for a moment I might say that I am delighted to see the hon. member for Cariboo listening intently, as he always does during the discussion of agricultural subjects. I wish to give the house of piece of interesting information, of which perhaps it has not been aware before. The hon. member for Cariboo, I understand, is a graduate of the Red Star livery grain and feed stable, and he could write a thesis on "The horses I have known". I am glad to see the hon. member here today.
I do want to say a few words about our policy. First of all, let it be clearly understood that the members of this party are firm supporters of the economic family farm unit. We believe in the dignity of the individual, and we believe this is one way of maintaining it in this country. We believe in the very definite values of rural life which are being discarded in many quarters today for a less satisfactory way of life. We believe that the family farm could be and should be an economic production unit, and could be made so at the present time by each farmer having the necessary acreage of good land, the necessary machinery and the requisite skill in management. We also believe this way of life provides the opportunity to practice democratic planning and in

so doing derive the benefits of the application of the principles of the mixed economy in which we believe.
There is a great opportunity here for the practice of these principles in our country life. It gives the opportunity for federal and provincial governments to plan, first of all, for conservation of our soil, forest and water resources in relation to agriculture. It gives the opportunity for planning in respect of research, which is very necessary and should be greatly increased. There should be more research in respect of production, and further research in respect of marketing. It gives also the opportunity for planning in respect of marketing legislation on both the federal and provincial levels. It gives the opportunity for planning a sound crop insurance scheme applicable to all branches of agriculture from the Atlantic to the Pacific. As a result of co-operation between federal and provincial governments the foundation in principle has been laid in the legislation passed by the house, but we believe it has to have wider application and apply to larger groups of people if the premiums are going to be such that the average farmer can pay them.
Now, the idea of the family farm unit also provides the opportunity for the development of co-operative ownership and, shall I say, the co-operative philosophy of life which has been so well illustrated in some Scandinavian and other western European countries. We could develop the co-operative ownership of processing plants and packing plants, as they are doing in the fruit industry. We could develop co-operative ownership of farm machinery where the investment is too large for a single farmer. This is happening in my own constituency, where fruit growers while owning some equipment, other expensive and heavy equipment is owned co-operatively. The co-operative packing house purchases it and it is owned co-operatively but used individually. This is another field that can be very well developed.
Then we have the development of farmers marketing in co-operation with federal and provincial planning and marketing boards. It also provides the opportunity for the government to co-operate even more closely than they do today with the farm organizations of this country. Finally, although we require this planning at federal and provincial levels and this extension of co-operative ownership in the ways I have mentioned, at the foundation we have the private ownership of the land by the farmer himself.
We believe that our program does provide the opportunity to practise the principles of the mixed economy in the co-operation of the farmers and their organizations. We believe

that development along these lines will provide basic security and maintain freedom, as well as lay the material foundation on which we can build a civilization that will provide the opportunity for the development of what I would term a genuine spiritual and cultural life.
Having dealt very briefly with the sort of over-all philosophy of our approach to agricultural policies and planning, I want to bring to the attention of the house the program for which this party stands, on what may be the last occasion before the advent of the day which, from our respective positions, we all look forward to or otherwise. The family farm is the basic unit of agricultural production and a desirable institution of our society. New Democratic objectives for agriculture are maximum food production for Canada and a hungry world, and effective marketing machinery to ensure fair and reasonable farm income.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, is this a debate on an estimate or an enunciation of a political party platform?

This is a debate on the administration estimate of the Department of Agriculture, and it has always been the accepted practice that we can deal with policy on this occasion. If the hon. gentleman is getting restless I can assure him that I am not going to speak at great length, because in this party we are in the habit of putting good things in small compass.
We believe that we must free the farmer from the effects of the cost-price squeeze, and that we must lower farm production costs by ending monopoly control over farm machinery, fertilizers, chemicals and other supplies. We also believe in the extension of long term loans at low interest; and to offset the adverse effects of vertical integration of farm processes by private companies we believe assistance should be given to farmers to build cooperatives for processing and marketing their own farm produce.
Our party will assure producers of sufficient marketing power by (a) development of federal producer marketing boards to coordinate the work of provincial marketing boards; (b) encouragement of co-operative and publicly sponsored facilities for storing, processing and distributing farm products; (c) development of programs to increase domestic levels of consumption; (d) distribution of surplus food to the needy of other lands in such a way as to avoid economic dislocation, and support for the establishment of a world food bank; (e) vigorous and imaginative efforts to sell surplus products such as wheat, including the acceptance of part payment in

sterling or currencies of other countries, longterm commodity agreements, credit arrangements, barter and other bilateral trade agreement; and (f), giving the wheat board permanent status.
I place this on the record as a brief summary of our policy, and with these few remarks I urge the government to consider this policy prior to the election period to see if it can embrace this policy which is the result of the thinking of farm organizations in co-operation with many segments of agriculture across Canada, and is the result of the experience and research of hon. members in this house and people from all parts of Canada.

subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext:
This discussion has developed into a very general consideration of rather broad agricultural questions. We have just listened to a statement by my good friend the hon. member for Kootenay West in which he said many things with which I am sure all hon. members are in wholehearted agreement.
The agricultural industry of this country is based on the family farm, and in my judgment anything which interferes with that unit as the basis of agriculture is not only against the interests of agriculture but is against the general interests of the people. We have heard a great deal about vertical integration and I am afraid we shall hear a great deal more bout it in the future. Policies and action must be forthcoming to arrest a trend which I am sure all those interested in the agricultural industry must fear. That trend is the encroachment of large corporations in a field of production which better serves the nation in the control and ownership of the farm family.
Steps will have to be taken to remove some of the heavy burdens that fall on agricultural producers. One of the burning issues, so far as agriculture is concerned in every province and municipality, is the very rapidly growing taxation burden on farm property, and this taxation burden is one of the costs which help drive the agricultural industry into vertical integration.
The Liberal party has given a great deal of thought to an agricultural program. Certain aspects of its program have already been made public, and further important, far reaching and advantageous planks in the Liberal platform will be made public in the days and weeks ahead. One of the things which is already public information is the policy of providing loans to municipalities at reasonable rates of interest in order to provide them with credit facilities which are not now available to them for undertaking the essential work that is part of municipal government.

Another important national plank has to do with the provision of crop insurance. The present government has a so-called crop insurance program which is not working across the nation. It is working to a very limited extent in the province of Manitoba, and to such a limited extent as to be of very little value in the province of Saskatchewan. It is not really working in any other place, and many improvements will have to be made to the crop insurance scheme before it can work successfully.
One of the things which needs to be done is for the federal and provincial governments interested in this field to expeditiously work out means by which there can be a real insurance against the great losses that might result from a crop insurance plan. As the formula is set up now, with the very limited contribution by the federal government, the major part of the burden of serious financial losses falls upon the farmers themselves and the provincial governments. This has brought the crop insurance scheme almost to a standstill and in many respects has made it an unworkable proposition.
Another plank in the Liberal platform which will have great appeal to western grain producers, and which is not a slogan or something directed merely to gaining popular support with little chance of being implemented, is the provision of the two price system for wheat. This is a well considered part of the Liberal program, and on the advent to power of a Liberal government it will be inaugurated. Under the two price system, wheat consumed in Canada by Canadians will carry a parity price, a price higher than the international price. This will implement a unanimous demand by farm organizations for a two price system, and the benefits from this system will be paid to the agricultural producers on the basis of certain deliveries, so that the financial benefits will be divided among the producers in a more equitable fashion than if they were paid on a strictly per bushel basis for all deliveries.
Those are some of the planks that have already been made public. Others will be forthcoming, and they will be forthcoming on the basis of a responsible program that will be placed on the statute books of this country in due course.

Another question I would like to raise today is this. I appreciate the difficulty of the parliamentary secretary in answering or trying to comment upon some of these general propositions. There is one parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture in his seat. If anyone has any information on this question, I would like it given to this committee after I conclude my remarks. There is a drought crisis on the prairies, of which all hon. members are fully aware, and there is a real possibility that there may be a second disastrous crop failure in western Canada this year. A disastrous crop failure this year following the disastrous crop failure in 1961 would entail tremendous hardship for western farmers since their financial reserves have already been largely depleted. The surplus of grain built up on the farms over a number of years has largely gone. The government has decided-and everyone is in favour of this-to make as many payments as possible to the farmers in as short a time as possible. If there is a crop failure this year the amount of income that farmers will have will be exceedingly small.
There is another crisis in the west that is being superimposed upon this drought crisis. I refer to the forecast of one of the largest grasshopper and cutworm infestations in the history of western Canada. This is a further danger to the very limited prospects of a crop in western Canada in 1962. The farmers are very much aware of this crisis. It is a common topic; one hears farmers saying "What about the grasshopper forecast? What about possible cutworm damage? If we are lucky enough to have enough moisture in the ground for the crop to sprout, will the insects devour the crops, so that even if we get rains at a later date they will be of little advantage?"
There was a conference held in Regina on March 23. This conference was reported in the Regina Leader-Post of March 24. More than 450 persons crowded into the museum in Regina, representing municipalities, provincial government departments and the federal government. They discussed this crisis. My plea this afternoon to the parliamentary secretary is for the federal government to take some responsibility by assisting in the provision of the chemicals necessary to fight this plague. I mean financial assistance. I think this is exceedingly important. The cost of spreading dieldrin or sevin at first sight may not seem to be an exceedingly expensive proposition; it is from 15 cents to 25 cents per acre. However, that is only part of the cost. There is also the cost of application, and if there is a widespread outbreak of grasshoppers there will be farmers who will need to apply this chemical to the crops two or

three times. This is an operation that will cost-depending upon the method of application, whether the farmer has his own equipment or whether he has to hire it, whether or not he has to hire aeroplane service for air spraying-somewhere between 50 cents and $1 per acre. If a farmer has to do this two or three times it is a very heavy cost at a time when he has very limited financial resources.
This is the cost in connection with destroying grasshoppers. If the farmer has to spray for cutworms and uses dieldrin or other chemicals he has to increase the concentration four or five times, because cutworms have a heavy protection and it takes more poison to kill the cutworm than it does to kill the grasshopper. Therefore it will be a very expensive proposition to deal with the widespread cutworm infestation that is being forecast.
I know that last year the federal government, at the request of the government of Saskatchewan, provided some emergency aircraft, I believe through the Department of National Defence, to transport the chemicals from Toronto to Regina. But I think the federal government should do more.. I think the federal government should take a lead and should be prepared to pay 50 per cent of the cost of these chemicals so this heavy burden does not have to be borne by the farmers who have suffered one crop failure, who have very limited financial resources and who, if they have to pay these costs entirely themselves, will either have to go on relief to obtain aid through the municipalities or, worse still, will have to say "We cannot afford it; we will just have to let the crop go". This is a practical proposition, whether a farmer should try to salvage a crop, when he does not know whether there will be anything left of the crop a month or so hence, at a cost of quite a large sum of money, money that he very badly needs, whether he should gamble his last few dollars, or whether he should say "Well, I cannot afford to salvage this crop".
There are other costs that farmers have to face at that time of year. They have to go out and spray for weeds. I know from my own experience last year that a great many farmers decided they could not afford to spray for weeds because they were so short of money, with the end result that where they did not spray for weeds there was no crop at all, and farmers who did spray for weeds got a small crop of probably three or four bushels per acre and found that the spraying of weeds was a good investment.
I am not putting these remarks forward, Mr. Chairman, in any way to condemn the

Since this government took office a problem has developed with regard to these subsidies, arising from the fact that a limit of some $50,000 was placed on the subsidy in respect of cold storage facilities, compared with a total subsidy equal to one third of the total cost, which was the case before the government made the change. I have been given to understand that the reason the limit was placed on this subsidy was that an overabundance of cold storage warehouse space existed in the country, and it was therefore felt necessary to place some limit on the public funds being spent in this particular area.
I have no cause to complain in this regard, because I am not familiar with the agricultural production situation. However, I do say that this argument certainly does not apply in the case of fisheries products. I think it is most incorrect to lump together the paying of subsidies to cold storage warehouses intended for such different purposes as the preservation of agricultural products and of fisheries products. The circumstances are entirely different, and the fishing industry generally suffers as a result of this approach.
I know that for some months, in fact, ever since this change in policy was made, the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative has been attempting to get the government to reconsider its aproach and to look upon the construction of cold storage warehouses for fisheries products in a different light. We have asked about this in the house on a number of occasions. We have asked the Minister of Agriculture about it and we have also made representations to the Minister of Fisheries. We have spoken about it and written letters, but invariably we have received the same negative reply. As a result, as I say, the fishing industry suffers and people like those in the fishermen's co-operative are disappointed. This particular organization had made plans for the expansion of its cold storage warehouse, but when the members finally got around to taking practical steps they found themselves cut off because the government had changed the rules in the middle of the game.
I do not expect the parliamentary secretary will be able to tell us that the situation is to be changed right now. Perhaps if he could confer with some of the members of the cabinet he might get them to make an announcement. But I place this question before the government again. I point out the seriousness of this problem and I reiterate-because this seems the only way to get things done-

Supply-Agriculture
that it is the fishing industry which suffers because of the restriction which has been placed on this subsidy, restriction based entirely on the situation which existed with regard to agricultural products.

subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext: I do not think it is necessary for me to add very much to what the hon. member for Skeena has said. There are many subjects on which we do not agree, but on this one on which we certainly do. When we made representations to the Minister of Fisheries on this subject last year we hoped that even this slow moving government would correct this situation and place the administration of the cold storage subsidy as far as fishermen are concerned under the Minister of Fisheries, where it might receive sympathetic attention. I urge the parliamentary secretary to use all the influence he has with the Minister of Finance and with the Prime Minister to see whether even at this late date-and perhaps because of this late date-the government might wake up to the fact that there is a fishing industry in this country.

Mr. Chairman, on supplementary estimates No. 3 we discussed a particular matter I brought to the attention of the hon. lady with respect to the Indians of the Tsimpsean reserve in Skeena, British Columbia. At that time we went into the matter rather fully and the hon. lady indicated that she was going to recall the tenders as a result of the confusion which then existed. I am informed that the minister has received a number of communications, including a band council resolution and a letter and perhaps a telegram from the band itself, since a copy of a letter dated March 24 has been sent to me. I wonder whether the minister can advise the house as to the present situation, in view of the fact that it appears that the band council, with the en-dorsation of the band, unanimously passed a resolution on March 23 indicating that they are opposed to the calling of new tenders.
The committee may recall that it was suggested by myself and other hon. members, which suggestion was acceded to by the minister and certainly with our approval, that new tenders should be called. However, apparently the Indians whose property it is are not pleased with such a decision. In the Prince Rupert daily News of March 23 there is a headlined story of an interview with Chief Sampson of the band, in which he indicates that he desires that the unsuccessful bid of the two received should be accepted. From all correspondence and statements it appears that the chief bases this first of all on the band's understanding of this particular offer, the Beaufort bid, and on some of the items which I brought to the minister's attention, particularly reforestation and the road. Furthermore, the band council is also concerned that if new tenders are called almost a year may elapse, and as there was no work for these Indians last year they are concerned that there be immediate work and immediate development of their resources. I am further informed, and I have no support for this statement but perhaps the minister can verify it, that the short term export market at least for such timber is unsteady, and there may be some amount of pressure with respect to letting the contract immediately.
While I am on my feet I also wish to inquire of the minister whether certain remarks made
29, 1962	2295
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate have been followed up by her branch in any way. They had to do with consultation between her branch and the Department of Trade and Commerce with a view to obtaining some idea whether this and similar timber may be exportable and will receive an export permit, particularly in view of the fact that on June 26, 1960 the Prime Minister, when dealing with legislation providing for the creation of the Department of Forestry, quoted with great approval a recommendation of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters in the following words:
Your committee feels that Canada cannot afford to ignore a potential so great for lumber and pulp sales as is offered in the Orient and, therefore, it recommends that these markets be approached on an open minded basis.
Because the Prime Minister himself seemed to be aware of the necessity for expanding our markets in that regard, I wonder whether the minister can advise the committee whether there have been exploratory talks between the two departments with a view to ascertaining that such timber, no matter who cuts it, whether it be the Indians or someone else, will be exportable; because this will have a considerable effect on the price of the timber and the amount of any bid.
I should like it to be firmly understood that my view still is that because of the great confusion which developed over the awarding of this contract it would be preferable, as it always is in such cases, to call for new tenders, but I must confess that I am concerned about the Indians' concern and about their very clearly expressed resolution and desire to have a deal of which they know the specifics.
The minister told the committee a matter of a couple of weeks ago that she was sending a commissioner out there. The commissioner appears now to be speaking to the public press, according to reports. He was to go to the Indian band and explain both bids to them. He appears to have done this; at least there has been a sufficient lapse of time to do so. Nevertheless, under date of March 24 there is a letter, which I believe the minister has, from the band council in which these people are most explicit about desiring one particular bid to be accepted.
Now, I cannot suggest other than that this must cause the minister great concern. Certainly it causes concern to anyone who is interested in the two problems, the one of calling for new tenders and the other of satisfying the Indians. I wonder if on these points the minister would advise the committee what she plans to do and, in addition, whether she could advise us if anything has been

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration done by her department in consultation with the Department of Trade and Commerce about export permits.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the particular supplementary vote which is before us relates only to forest fire protection. As the hon. lady knows, the past year was a disastrous fire year throughout Canada, and this amount of $59,500 is required for unpaid accounts in five of the provinces.
In so far as the matter which the hon. lady raises is concerned, I might say to her that as of the present time new tenders have not been called. The representations which she has made will, of course, be considered in due course by the minister.

subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext: I do not want the parliamentary secretary to be under any misapprehension that I am making representations on behalf of any group except the Indians, according to their clearly expressed wishes in the resolution. Of course the minister is their trustee in this regard. I do not suggest in any way, that any decision that has to be made is easy, but I should hope the minister would be able to advise the committee just what she plans to do in view of the fact it is getting rather late in the season and apparently if there is any delay in the further calling of tenders, the Indians will suffer. The last time tenders were called it took almost a year from the time of the original negotiations until the time the tenders were received. If such a delay occurs now, then the Indians will be deprived of income, work and training. It is on their behalf that I am making these inquiries, and on behalf of no other person.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext: I am sure the hon. lady can be confident that the minister will take a decision based solely upon the good of the Indians who are involved.

subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext: I take it, then, she has made no decision.

subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext:
I do not wish to be unkind about it, but I should hope that the situation would be as represented by the parliamentary secretary. I should like to make a few brief comments on this problem because, unfortunately, I was absent when it arose earlier. However, I do not wish to get involved in the intricacies of the negotiations. Unfortunately the natives themselves, as I know from speaking with the Indian people, do not trust Commissioner Boys. I have had this view expressed to me by many of the Indian people at Fort Simpson, the Queen Charlotte islands and over on the Babine agency. They do not have that degree of trust in Commissioner Boys which is necessary for the proper conduct of negotiations between the

Indian affairs branch and the natives themselves. They do not feel particularly confident, either, about Mr. Brett. I do not know whether this results from a misunderstanding as between Mr. Brett and the band council itself or from the inability or failure of Mr. Brett to fully explain all that was taking place. It could be for some other reason entirely, but they do not have that degree of confidence in Mr. Brett which is necessary.
The lack of trust in these individuals is understandable, because the natives have been exploited by the so-called white people for many years. This has developed almost an inherent feeling of distrust for any of our dealings. I am very much afraid of what might happen in this particular instance if there is anything in the future which smacks of dishonesty or which leads to misunderstanding. If the situation should arise the band might well say "All right, we will just keep the timber" and the Indians will remain in economic stagnation for another 10 or 15 years. This is the greatest fear I have as to what could result from the situation which exists there.
Incidentally, this feeling is not confined to Fort Simpson. There are other villages involved in the sale of timber, and they have had relationships with Mr. Boys and Mr. Brett. These people are also now a bit reluctant and concerned about how far they should go in these particular negotiations. It would be my thought that the recent attitude expressed by the band council in the letter to which reference was made should be the point of view that should carry the most weight with the department. This was a unanimous decision of the band itself, but Mr. Boys expressed some disagreement and said it was not unanimous. Evidently the band expressed some preference for one of the two bidders in connection with the sale of this timber.
Perhaps it may be necessary to engage outside legal counsel-I know the band has consulted lawyers-to ensure that the interest of the people there are protected to the fullest possible extent. I am not sure whether this step may be necessary now. I am afraid that unless this is done the results may be injurious to the band itself, and could very easily contribute to the destruction of that mutual trust we are trying to develop between ourselves and the native people of this nation. This mutual trust is difficult to establish because the history of our dealings with these people is not particularly clean.
In my opinion our sole concern should be to protect the interests of the Indians to the fullest possible extent and to move toward the development of this mutual feeling of

trust. Unfortunately, as' I say, whether it was deliberate, by reason of inefficiency or just misunderstanding, the native people in Tsimpsean and elsewhere do not have that degree of trust in Commissioner Boys or Mr. Brett which is so necessary. Neither do they have a very high regard for Mr. Ewen, the officer in charge of the Skeena river agency which covers the particular area.

subtopic: REPORTED LAY-OFF OF EMPLOYEES OF DEVELOPMENT AND ENGINEERING BRANCH
speechtext:
I should like to direct some questions to the minister in respect of this matter. I have been informed that there was a company created on the west coast called Nishka Pacific Forest Products, a company which was composed entirely of Indians and which chose to apply to cut timber on the Nass reserve. I understand they were told by Paul Brett, the forester for the branch in British Columbia, that if they were ever entitled to cut the timber they would have to replant the areas which they cut.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-33, to amend the National Energy Board Act (drainage works).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill was brought before the house previously on December 13, 1960. By reference to the debate on that date the arguments presented at that time are available to the members of the house. The bill presented this year is similar in all respects to that presented in 1960. It provides as follows:
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
1.	Subsection (1) of section 75 of the National Energy Board Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"75.	(1) Sections 207 to 246, section 248 and
section 273 of the Railway Act, in so far as they are reasonably applicable and not inconsistent with this act, apply mutatis mutandis to companies and their works and undertakings."
Then section 2 of the proposed amendment would repeal section 77 of the National Energy Board Act and substitute the following therefor:
"77. (1) Except a drain used to drain land that for the purpose of municipal assessment is classed as a farm, market garden, or nursery, no highway, private road, railway, irrigation ditch, drain, drainage ditch, sewer, telegraph, telephone line or line for the transmission of hydrocarbons, power or any other substance shall, except by leave of the board, be carried across, along, upon or under any pipe line.
The history of section 273 of the Railway Act, which the amendment aims to have included in the National Energy Board Act, would make pipe lines operating under federal charter subject to provincial drainage laws as are pipe lines operating under provincial charter.
Back in 1903 this house spent many days debating an amendment to the Railway Act as it existed at that time in order that farmers might be adequately protected against large railway corporations when it came to settling drainage crossings on railway properties. Our Canadian sense of fair play provides that those in a contest should have equal ability; that is to say, we do not pit a large corporation against a small private individual. That procedure is not fair. In 1903 the debates surrounding the advisability of introducing or creating section 273 of the Railway Act centred around that principle. It was felt that individual farmers and drainage authorities had neither the resources nor the wealth to contest successfully the points of law and points of advantage with the great railway corporations of those days. The net result was that section 273 was incorporated into the Railway Act in order to compel the railways to carry across railway property, at the expense of the railway, farm drains and drains provided for by drainage authorities. When the Pipe Lines Act was set up, although 40 some sections of the Railway Act which involved provisions for the expropriation of land and settlement for the same were incorporated into the Pipe Lines Act, section 273 of the Railway Act was left out. Therefore the individual farmer and drainage authorities in the various parts of Canada were left to fight an unequal battle against the great pipe line corporations.
When the National Energy Board Act was introduced in 1959 and passed by the house, again section 273 of the Railway Act was

omitted, although 40 some sections of the Railway Act were incorporated in the National Energy Board Act. Having regard to the way in which the act is being administered, it is now felt that section 273 should be incorporated into the National Energy Board Act. It is felt that the provisions of section 273 of the Railway Act are just as necessary today in the National Energy Board Act to protect individual farmers and drainage authorities against the great pipe line corporations as the provisions of that section of the Railway Act were necessary back in 1903 to protect the farmers and drainage authorities of those days.
As an indication of the attitude of the pipe line companies, I might say that there are now four pipe lines crossing Middlesex West. Three of them operate under provincial charter and therefore are subject to the provisions contained in section 273 of the Railway Act. In other words, they are subject to provincial drainage regulations. One of the four pipe lines which crosses Middlesex West, Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, operates under a federal charter and does not come under the provisions of the provincial drainage legislation of Ontario. The result is that when a farm drain or a municipal drain has to be run across the right of way of any one of the three pipe lines of Sun oil, Imperial oil and Union gas, those three lines must pay the extra cost which is occasioned by their presence or operation there. There is no question that they pay these costs and as far as I know everyone seems quite happy with the situation.
However, Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, operating under a federal charter, does not come under these provincial drainage regulations as contained in section 273 of the Railway Act, with the result that they do not pay the costs of such crossings. They assess these costs against the individual farmer or against the municipal drainage authority.
It is true that up to the present time, with one exception as far as I know, individual farmers and drainage authorities who have constructed drains across the right of way of Interprovincial Pipe Line Company have agreed to the conditions laid down by that company which assess the whole cost against the farmer or the drainage authority.
I should like to outline the conditions laid down by Interprovincial Pipe Line Company with respect to such crossings and to do so I should like to place on the record a letter from Interprovincial Pipe Line Company to Archibald, Gray and McKay, Ontario land surveyors, London, Ontario, dated January 21, 1960. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether I could have permission to have this letter 26207-1-1474

Notwithstanding the foregoing, all work which might disturb the pipe, which necessitates re-aligning, raising or lowering the pipe or excavating material from over or round it, or the addition of casing or other appurtenances thereto, shall be performed by the company, and all costs and expenses of such work shall be borne and paid by the authority having control over such drain, or the owner thereof, as the case may be.
2.	The authority having control over the drain, or the owner thereof, shall at all times maintain its crossing of the company's pipe line in good working order and condition, so that at no time shall any damage be caused to the company's pipe line or its usefulness or safety be impaired, or the full use and enjoyment thereof be in any way interfered with.
3.	Subject to the proviso hereinafter set out, before any work of constructing, renewing or repairing its crossing of the company's pipe line is begun, the authority having control over such crossing or the party making, owning or operating such crossing, as the case may be, shall give to the company at least 48 hours notice thereof in writing, to enable the company to appoint an inspector to see that the work is performed in such a manner as shall, in all respects, comply with this order; except that in cases of emergency, the appropriate official of the company shall be notified immediately. The amount of wages and expenses of such inspector shall be paid by the authority having control over such drain, or the owner thereof, as the case may be, upon receipt

from the company of a statement showing in reasonable detail the particulars of such wages and expenses.

The applicant shall at all times wholly indemnify the company from and against all loss, costs, damage, injury and expense to which the company may be put by reason of any damage or injury to persons or property caused by the drain construction, maintenance or operation of the drain, as well as against any damage or injury resulting from the imprudence, neglect or want of skill of the employees or agents of the applicant in connection with the construction, operation, maintenance, renewal or repair of said drain, or any other works herein provided for, unless the cause of such loss, cost, damage, injury or expense can be traced elsewhere.
Those are the conditions requested by Interprovincial Pipe Line Company in connection with any order which the board shall issue for a private individual or drainage authority to carry a drain across their pipe. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these conditions are heavily weighted in favour of the pipe line company and offer little or no protection to the farmer or drainage authority concerned.
Any crossings which have been made to date have been made under these conditions. So far as I am aware, all the costs of drains carried across interprovincial pipe lines have been paid for by the farmer or drainage authority concerned. However, three pipe lines have expended as much as $7,000 or $8,000 per crossing in expenses in order to carry drains across their line, and there has been no question about who should pay those costs. All pipe lines operating under provincial charter pay all the extra costs when any farm drain of an individual farmer or drainage authority crosses their line. It is suggested that, in all fairness and justice, this anomaly should be removed and that all pipe lines should be treated alike. This amendment, therefore, is proposed to the National Energy Board Act in an effort to see that any discrimination is removed and that the pipe line companies have to give the same deal to all farmers and drainage authorities concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a few short and personal comments following the statement of the hon. member. I examined Bill No. C-33, an act to amend the National Energy Board Act (drainage works), and I must say that I want to express some rather significant reservations on the matter.
I have no doubt that in submitting this bill, the hon. member has a very praiseworthy aim, and that its effects might, in some cases, be of great benefit to farmers.
I believe that this is, primarily a local is-


sue, for which it would seem possible to find a solution without resorting to such drastic amendments.
But I do not object so much to that as to the way of going about it, which, to my mind, is prejudicial to provincial rights in that regard.
We are dealing here with drainage works, and I think that the hon. member who preceded me will admit that there is nothing more local and provincial than drainage works. The explanatory notes to the bill, and more particularly the last two paragraphs, speak for themselves in that respect, and I quote:
The result of the present laws is that the railway utilities, interprovincial and provincial, and the provincial pipe lines utilities are subject to provincial drainage authorities while the interprovincial and international pipe line utilities are subject to the national energy board.
This bill proposes to incorporate in the National Energy Board Act the provincial drainage laws so as to apply these laws to interprovincial and international pipe lines with respect to farms, market gardens and nurseries so classed under the applicable provincial assessment law.
In other words, and to summarize the scope of this bill, what is intended here is the incorporation in a federal act, by way of an amendment, of all provincial drainage laws.
In my opinion, it will be necessary to redefine farms, market gardens and nurseries. It can readily be seen how these definitions, for the purposes of municipal assessments, can vary from one province to another.
I fail to see how such a bill could be approved without the province having been consulted on the matter. I want to point out that we seem to forget too often that the provinces hold annual sessions, through interprovincial conferences. Thanks to the leadership of the premier of the province of Quebec, discussion with the provinces is much more easy now.
Too often, in passing measures of this kind which we considered by ourselves, we confront the provinces with a fait accompli.
It may be that we are faced with technical problems-this might well be so in this case- and that the co-operation of the provinces is not only desirable but necessary.
I submit that in any field of joint federal-provincial jurisdiction, and especially in any field of purely local and provincial jurisdiction, we should have here, in the House of Commons, some machinery which would prevent the repeated introduction of certain bills

which I feel exceed our jurisdiction and which, even if they were adopted, would be ultra vires and could not be carried out.
Mr. Speaker, I think there is a rather easy way of overcoming such a difficulty.
We all know that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) is authorized since the Canadian Bill of Rights has been passed to examine bills introduced in this house to satisfy himself that they are not contrary to any provision of the bill of rights. Therefore, I feel that the bill now before us would not have been introduced if such a check had been made.
In any field involving federal and provincial jurisdictions, I wonder why the Minister of Justice as well as the officials of his department would not be authorized to examine the bills before their introduction to see if they are not encroaching upon the exclusive privileges of the provinces.
I think that if that was done, many a difficulty could be prevented.
I do not want to take too much of the time of the house, because I wish to give other members the opportunity to comment on this bill.
May I simply be allowed to sum up. The intention here is to incorporate provincial drainage laws in a federal statute, and from the explanatory notes I read a moment ago, I am inclined to question the constitutionality of the bill.
However, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) for having introduced this bill. I believe that his purpose is very commendable, and that it would be in the interest of a very large number of our fellow citizens that something be done along those lines, so that drainage projects may be carried out in the most practical way for all farmers and landowners through whose lands those pipe lines pass.
In my opinion, it would be possible to find a more practical and easier solution, a solution which would certainly be more constitutional than this bill introduced by the hon. member.

speechtext:
On rising to speak briefly about this bill I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) who has brought this matter to our attention again. Contrary to the views expressed by the previous speaker, I believe it is a matter which we should seriously consider passing.
With vast resources of gas and oil in western Canada and with major markets for it in the east, it will mean that in the
National Energy Board Act future we will have many more pipe lines bringing gas and oil to eastern Canada. I should like to give my interpretation of the bill. Its intention is to amend the National Energy Board Act so that the construction of pipe lines will come within the provisions of the provincial statutes and be subject to provincial drainage laws and to the judicial interpretation of these laws by the courts, regardless of whether the pipe lines are constructed under a provincial or federal charter.
In past years we have not had too much of a problem in connection with oil and gas pipe lines constructed under federal charter because there were not too many of them. However this is now becoming a factor which we must consider. At the present time there are several bills coming before the house in connection with the construction of gas and oil pipe lines through different parts of Canada and for that reason I think it is most important we should consider this bill and give it some measure of approval. With the advance of time there are other problems to be considered, probably not particularly connected with this bill, but there is also the building of underground power transmission lines and telephone lines under federal charter, that cross more than one province.
Surely it is only reasonable that the national energy board drainage regulations should be amended to comply with provincial drainage regulations? I do not intend to deal with the mechanics of the bill. I believe the hon. member for Middlesex West has done that in a very able manner, but I would like to outline some of the problems which appear to me in connection with the building of pipe lines. For instance there is the disruption of a land tile drainage system, which is a most important matter in the province of Ontario, more especially where we have fruit and vegetable growers.
I understand that a 30-inch pipe line, which is a common size for the bigger projects, has to be placed about six to eight feet deep in the ground, and the trench must be quite wide to provide working space while the pipe line is being built. One can readily understand the problem there. But even in the case of a pipe line of much less capacity the flow of a field tile drainage system could be completely disrupted and could only be made to operate satisfactorily by the construction of an interceptor tile drainage system on either side of the pipe line. I have some experience in connection with this and I know it is a problem which could lead to a lot of expense.
Unless the construction of pipe lines is brought under the regulations of provincial
2306	HOUSE OF
National Energy Board Act drainage laws this expense could very easily fall to the responsibility and cost of the farmers and wheat growers whose land is crossed by a pipe line. I also contend that pipe lines for the transmission of gas and oil should come under the regulations of provincial drainage laws for the purpose of being made subject to special assessments for clearing and repairing natural water courses, just the same as other structures and assessable prop-perties above ground. Occasionally water courses have to be cleared and repaired, and when that is done an assessment is made under the authority of provincial drainage law and it is assessed against the adjacent properties concerned. Should federal pipe lines be excluded from provincial drainage regulations it is quite possible they might not have to share part of this cost.
There is also damage caused by interference with natural water courses and spring flooding conditions, which often cannot be calculated until wash-outs and flooding take place. Provision can best be made to provide for these hazards under provincial drainage laws.
There is another matter I wish to raise and it is one which is not entirely relevant to this bill. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, if I get out of order you will correct me. I have made some study of this matter and I recommend to the national energy board that they take into consideration ways and means to recover to Canada-where facilities are available and where there is a requirement-a proportion of the huge quantities of Canadian gas and oil that may be piped into the United States from points west of Port Arthur. This gas and oil is transshipped by a great network of pipe lines across the United States, and I understand some of it arrives back in Canada, and I suppose at substantially increased costs.
I have checked with the national energy board and have been advised that no recovery provisions have yet been made in export permits for gas and oil. However, they agree it is a matter well worth considering.
Mr. Speaker, I could say more on this matter but I know other hon. members wish to speak on it. I think that as far as the province of Ontario is concerned this bill is a matter that should be given very favourable consideration. As the mover of the bill has mentioned it is connected with the old Railway Act which was brought in many, many years ago. We have to review these matters from time to time and, as I have already said, because of the large number of gas and oil pipe lines that are coming to eastern Canada we should take steps now to see that those with federal charters come within the provincial drainage schemes.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVINCIAL DRAINAGE LAWS TO PIPE LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join previous speakers in this debate in congratulating the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) for the work he has done in the preparation of this bill and for the discussion that has ensued from it.
I believe we are all very worried when we hear or read of the terms and requirements that are made by pipe line companies. We have heard read this afternoon correspondence from an interprovincial pipe line and we heard the terms they made when they had the opportunity of evading some of the responsibilities that other pipe lines have to face. These are legal terminologies, it is true; but they remind me of reading the original contracts which farmers signed in many cases, and the heavy legal verbiage which allowed absolutely no loophole whatever to anyone connected with the contract. I think a farmer is terrified by the language itself and therefore when he makes any request he is, and rightly should be, always very cautious when approaching any problem in connection with pipe lines.
It is perfectly true that in Ontario there is going to be a continuing and growing demand for drainage and that where drainage crosses a pipe line it is going to be highly essential that this drainage be carried out at the lowest possible cost to the municipality, the authority or the farmer who may be involved in the drainage program. For the success and progress of our agricultural industry it is necessary that drainage shall take place on a much larger scale than has been necessary in the past. For this reason we must be concerned with the advent of gas pipe lines passing through the agricultural lands of Ontario. I have been concerned with the trend that has been indicated by at least one speaker today. He indicated that we should use as the basis of our argument the fact that the province of Ontario or other provinces have passed drainage laws in a provincial sense, and because the federal act has not been sufficient to take care of this problem in the past we should make all pipe lines into provincial lines so that they would be under provincial jurisdiction and the provincial governments, having jurisdiction over both fields, would find less difficulty in equalizing the problem as between the drainage act and the Pipe Lines Act. I suggest that this is a dangerous thing to do because, as the last speaker pointed out, there is an increasing growth in Canada, not only of lines carrying oil and other commodities in the province, but there is also a very large and growing field of international and interprovincial pipe lines.

Our laws must be brought into line. I think this is really what would happen if the amendments contained in this bill were put into effect.
I agree with those who say that this may be a very cumbersome way of doing it. It may be true that we would have to go back to the Railway Act and pick out some of the sections that should not necessarily have been applied, but I think this has been made necessary by the very inflexibility of the pipe lines with which we deal. The Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, and particularly Trans Canada Pipe Line Limited have shown their inflexibility in any type of dealing not covered by the contract they originally signed. In my opinion these original contracts had the best legal brains in the country behind them and the pipe line companies had at their beck and call the best kind of legal advice in drawing them up.
I am always amused to remember that the only thing that was not put into the bill concerning the trans-Canada pipe line was a complete and workable expropriation clause. How they could have missed the most important one, I do not know, because I am sure from reading many of these contracts that the pipe line companies employed the best legal brains they could afford. I think it is a condemnation of the legal advice that pipe lines receive when it is necessary for the hon. member for Middlesex West to ask parliament today to enact laws that will provide for the very simple matter of allowing water to flow from one area to another and surmount the difficulties created by pipe lines. It is perfectly true that the pipe line companies have expropriated, bought or own the particular strip of land under which they have put their pipe line. But this does not give them the almighty right to say, "We will not allow any other type of development in the area". They were able to look far enough ahead and see that there would not be a loophole which would mean they would have to give some assistance to the farmers and they have relied upon their contracts when this question has arisen.
I think the farmer has a right, if he is draining the back 40 acres of his farm to another area of the farm, to say to the pipe line company, "You are obstructing this drainage". He should be able to say this, as he can when a highway is involved. I think the farmer should have the right to say, "You must put in the connecting link in my drainage system. This is your responsibility. You are now a member of the community. You are part of this area. This should be done".
I think it is a condemnation of this whole industry that we should have to come to parliament and ask, in what I consider to be
National Energy Board Act a very roundabout way, for a very simple and basic need to be provided, namely the need for drainage in rural areas. I believe that the pipe line companies would find a great many more friends in parliament and across the country if they did not try to beat the little farmer but instead co-operated with him in connection with the rights they obtained when buying these narrow strips of land under which they buried their pipe lines.
I suggest they should always be responsible for the particular area and putting in the connecting link, because I think it would be unfair to ask the farmer to dig up the pipe line and put in the connecting link himself. I think this would be dangerous. I think it would not be in the interests of safety if he had to do this, particularly if there happened to be some rock there and he decided to use force to remove the obstruction. I think everyone will agree that this is going to have to be done by the company itself, and the company should carry the expense of maintaining their interest and participation in the community in co-operation with the other members of the community, who in most cases happen to be farmers whose land they are crossing, and in some cases dividing, by their pipe line. I hope we will not give any consideration to this idea of dividing into provincial jurisdictions the pipe lines that are interprovincial in nature. I believe the federal government has a responsibility for maintaining liaison with the provincial governments and for giving whatever direction may be necessary by way of regulations or other means, such as the bill now before us, to assure farmers and other members of the community, including drainage authorities, that they will have free access to this type of land so that drainage can be completed. It is well known that the presence of a pipe line does not mean that the whole topography of an area is changed and that water will begin to flow in another direction.
The house has an opportunity of passing this measure this afternoon so that its provisions may be put speedily into effect. It is unfortunate that it should be necessary to proceed in this way by adding a section to the act which would allow the drainage authorities the same rights as they would have enjoyed if we had been dealing with a highway, a railroad or some other obstruction. Years ago it was necessary to deal with this problem while the railways were being laid. I should have thought that the improvement in public relations since then would have allowed us to deal with the present difficulties in a much more friendly manner. However, if that is not the case I shall certainly support the proposed amendment and I hope other members of the committee will do likewise.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVINCIAL DRAINAGE LAWS TO PIPE LINES
speechtext:
As has
been indicated, this bill deals with amendments to the National Energy Board Act to make pipe lines operating under federal charter, that is, interprovincial and even international pipe lines, subject to the drainage laws of the provinces through which the pipe lines pass. It is suggested that for this purpose section 273 of the Railway Act be added to the 49 sections of the Railway Act already incorporated in section 75 (1) of the National Energy Board Act.
I have had very little experience indeed, I must confess, with this type of problem but when I heard there was this strange difference between the procedure required to get compensation from interprovincial pipe line companies as compared with the relatively simple and expeditious procedure involved in provincial pipe lines, I was amazed. I think this anomaly, this omission, must obviously have been due to inadvertence rather than design. I can see all sorts of problems involved with which municipalities and farms will have to contend increasingly even in eastern Ontario, questions which are fertile of litigation; whether, for instance, a pipe line under construction should go under or over existing trunk sewer or even a farm tiled drainage system. Every three or five years these drains have to be cleaned out and maintained. Surely, if one of these ditches intersects an oil pipe line, the company should be responsible for contributing a portion of the cost of this maintenance. There are many other instances where these difficulties arise. Many, as I say, are fertile of litigation. Nevertheless, that is an expensive course to take both in time and in the cost involved and as has been suggested people tend to be, if you will, almost terrified by the prospects of having to contend with highly paid legal counsel, the best available advice, such as the pipe line companies can afford.
In wet regions and especially in certain parts of Ontario, surplus water gathers in low spots in the fields and this interferes with cultivation and ruins standing crops. Proper drainage is the answer to this condition. Even in our own area of Cornwall tile drainage will become increasingly common. This drainage is provided by placing stone tiles end to end in a trench approximately two feet below the surface of the land. Surface water seeps into the drain and is carried away into suitable outlets, usually into larger drains and ultimately into open ditches. This permits the aeration of the soil and allows a healthy crop to grow. It also helps the cultivation of the soil.
I see that time is passing fast. I just want to emphasize, since I shall not be able to


finish the remarks I wish to make, that these proposed amendments to the National Energy Board Act were endorsed by the Ontario association of land surveyors at their annual meeting which was held in Hamilton in February, 1960. I think it is interesting that one of the gentlemen who took part in those discussions at that time is a friend and former classmate of mine from Cornwall, Mr. Leonard Stidwell. I think it is important that we should anticipate these difficulties before they become acute and therefore I think it is highly desirable that this legislation should be incorporated into the National Energy Board Act so as to provide an expeditious, quick, efficient, cheap and familiar method of dealing with this problem.

There is another reason for putting this request at this time. Unlike former sessions, there has been no sitting of the external affairs committee, an arrangement that has enabled us to pursue interrogations in past years, and which therefore eliminated unnecessary duplication of discussion in the house. Apart altogether from the desirability of having ministers conduct the discussion of these various estimates themselves, to which course the government has registered a very strong and totalitarian objection-I say that with no offence because we are in a very happy and constructive mood tonight-I think that the parliamentary secretary should accede readily to the suggestion that we postpone until tomorrow item 692 and the following items under external affairs up to 706. If there is any difference of opinion then as to the procedure to be followed we could have that argument at that time. I simply request at this time that the parliamentary secretary forgo dealing with these matters until the return to the house of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I want to support wholeheartedly the most reasonable plea of the hon. member for Essex East that

the estimates of the Department of External Affairs be postponed until the minister returns, which I understand he will do tomorrow.
Tonight.

But it will be possible for him to be present tomorrow. In view of the fact that the committee on external affairs has not sat this session and in view of the excellent work the Secretary of State for External Affairs has been doing at Geneva, I think it would be most unfortunate if this house were to pass these estimates without having a report from him. I am sure we are all looking forward to hearing of his activities at Geneva, and we on this side again look forward to extending our co-operation to the government through constructive suggestions for the improvement of our foreign policy. I do urge the parliamentary secretary to give consideration to our pleas.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Essex East knows how very difficult it is for me ever to resist his blandishments, and when they are supported by the hon. member for Kootenay West it is all the more difficult. But this is an occasion when I must indicate that what they have suggested would be in fact a departure from what has been the practice of the committee of supply.
We had some discussion yesterday as to what has been the practice in dealing with final supplementary estimates. In all instances they have been dealt with not by the individual ministers concerned, with one or perhaps two exceptions, I think, but by the Minister of Finance whose poor substitute I am on this particular occasion. The custom and tradition of the committee have never been to use the final supplementary estimates for statements of policy of the type to which the hon. member for Essex East refers.
The final supplementary estimates generally, and in this case in particular, as my friend will see, deal with the provision of further amounts. The policy has been determined earlier by the committee. The issue which is before the committee in these instances is the wisdom or otherwise of supplementing amounts, and that is why these estimates are called supplementary estimates. If we were to concede the point of view of the hon. member for Essex East, then in each instance the minister of the crown whose estimates they were would be in the house for these final supplementary estimates.
I think perhaps the best statement that has been made in respect of the procedure in this regard was made by that very distinguished minister of finance, Mr. Justice Abbott. Over 26207-1-1481
Supply-External Affairs the dinner hour I sought to find the statement he made on one occasion when he was minister of finance. I believe that during all the time he was minister he conducted the final supplementaries himself. I know that in the election year of 1953 the final supplementaries, with almost as many items as there are at the present time, went through in less than one afternoon.
To concede what my hon. friends suggest would be a departure from the tradition, custom and practice of this committee, and difficult as it is for me to resist the hon. member for Essex East when he is in one of his rare reasonable moods, I regret that I have to do so tonight.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sure that the decision just made by the parliamentary secretary involved great concern and discernment on his part.
