He has given certain reasons for his position, but I want to bring to his attention one or two points that I think differentiate the position in which we find ourselves tonight from that to which my hon. friend has made reference. He says it is the custom and tradition of this house in dealing with supplementary estimates not to have the ministers in their seats to answer questions. That statement-*

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-is not wholly accurate because I can remember full well further supplementary estimates when I had to come into the house at the request of the then minister of finance to explain certain matters concerning items under the heading of the Department of Transport. I can think of two particular instances right now where there would have been a terrific row if I had not been here and I will bring them to the attention of the parliamentary secretary if need be.
The other point I wish to bring to his attention is that the circumstances today are entirely different from those to which my hon. friend has reference. First, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as the hon. member for Essex East has said, has been at an important conference in Geneva and I think he would be one of the first to want to be in the house to discuss these items. The minister has been away for some time on important government business and it seems to me that the house would welcome his presence here. Knowing him as I do, I am sure that he too would want to be here to give an explanation of these items. I am also satisfied in my own mind that if he were here they would go through much faster.
However, leaving that aside and without assenting for the moment to what my hon. friend has said, let me say to him that the

Supply-External Affairs circumstances today are entirely different from those to which he refers because, as has been succinctly put by the hon. member for Essex East, we do not know how long we are going to be here. Having regard to these circumstances, if it is a fact that this is the last opportunity we will have to discuss estimates then it is our duty and responsibility to ascertain what these expenditures are for. It is also our duty and responsibility-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be glad to tell the hon. member.
Does my hon. friend really seriously contend-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have not finished yet. I want to say, if that is the case, as I have every reason to believe it is, then I think we should know, a fortiori, what these things refer to.
There is another reason, a far more important reason, which was raised by my hon. friend yesterday. It has to do with the manner in which these supplementary estimates No. 4 have been compiled. If you look at them and compare them with No. 3, you will find there is no reason for having a discussion of these estimates at this time. If they had been prepared with due order and without the confusion to which I referred the other day in a question addressed to the Minister of Finance, all except perhaps a few of them could have been included in supplementary estimates No. 3. If you look at No. 3, and compare it with No. 4, you will find the titles are practically the same and the items are practically the same. There is little or no difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not want to take up an undue amount of the time of the house, but I have marked here in red ink the duplicate items. If my hon. friend insists, I will give him the items that are contained in supplementary estimates 3 and 4.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There are five.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend says there are five. I refer to supplementary estimates No. 4, items 677 to 682, which are under the production and marketing branch; then there is land rehabilitation, irrigation and water storage projects, and these are the same as in estimates No. 3. The items in external affairs are in large part a duplication. They are not the same items; that is not what I intended to say, but they are a duplication. The point I am trying to make is that these estimates should have been ready and prepared and included in supplementary estimates No. 3 rather than in No. 4 because there is a period of barely three weeks

between the time No. 3 was tabled in this house and the time No. 4 was tabled.
There is an added reason why it seems to me that there has not been the order in the preparation of these estimates that normally there is under conditions of this kind. For these reasons, I again ask the parliamentary secretary if he will not give consideration to the point which was raised by the hon. member for Essex East.

Before the parliamentary secretary replies and so that he will not repeat a statement that he could not support, I turned up the only volume of Hansard I happened to have on my desk. I looked at page 2402 of Hansard for 1957, volume III, and I read:
Supply: The house in committee of supply. Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair. Department of Citizenship and Immigration, Immigration Branch-553.
Field and inspectional service, Canada-further amount required, $194,177.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What date was that?

March 18, 1957, the last further supplementaries brought into this house by my friend Mr. Harris. There was a question by Mr. Knowles, a reply by me and then pages and pages thereafter of discussion in which Mr. Harris took no part but in which I took a part. This was only characteristic of what happened whenever hon. members in the opposition in those days wanted information from a minister. The difference, as my hon. friend from Laurier has pointed out, between the situation in the days when hon. gentlemen were over here and we were over there and the hon. member for Carleton and I most of the time were out of the house, was that our supplementaries were supplementaries. They were not a complete new budget. This is a new feature of this government this year. As I pointed out yesterday, in all, the further supplementaries added together from the year ending March 31, 1953 to March 31, 1957, all the further supplementaries added together in those five years were $357 million and the further supplementaries for 1961-62 are $341 million for this one year, nearly as much as the last five years before 1957.
Well, this means you are bringing in a new budget. You are upsetting the ways and means. It means the Minister of Finance had no notion, as we know he did not last year, of what he was doing at all. Never before that I have been able to discover have four sets of further supplementaries been introduced. Perhaps this happened in Mr. Bennett's day, but never again as far as I have been able to ascertain. The whole point is that we no longer have any ways and means at all in this house. We no longer have any balance.

This government, in order to create phoney impressions of balance of ways and means at budget time deliberately vastly underestimated; then the Prime Minister has some vision and we get a whole lot of entirely new expenditures introduced into this house as further supplementary estimates.
These are huge sums of money, almost as much as the budgets were in the days before the second world war. We say that we would like one department in these estimates held up for a perfectly good reason. After all, sir, it is not every day or even every year, although unfortunately it happens all too often because they do not seem to be very successful, that we have a disarmament conference under the terms and conditions of this one and in the state the world is in at this time. It seems to me, sir, a very unwise denial of a reasonable request. I realize how awkward it is for the parliamentary secretary when the premier of British Columbia snaps his fingers and the Minister of Finance has to go trotting out to British Columbia to bow and scrape before that great potentate. I realize how embarrassing it is for the parliamentary secretary, who may be ticked off, who may even be fired like Mr. Coyne-
Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would it not be well for the hon. gentleman to get back to discussing these estimates?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I wonder if I could have the floor just for a moment? I was not in the chair when this discussion got under way, and I did not realize that the basis for it, as has been explained to me by the Clerk of the house, was that hon. members wanted this series of items on external affairs deferred. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate came back to that point just a moment ago. I feel that debate on this subject has been fairly well exhausted and unless the parliamentary secretary accedes I think it would be well if we got back to the item under consideration, which is departmental administration and which allows fairly wide scope for debate.

You interrupted me, Mr. Chairman, just as I was going to do what I think you will not deny I have a perfect right to do. I was going to appeal to the senior minister who is now leading the house. It is the ministers of the crown and not the parliamentary secretary who must make a decision on this matter. The senior minister, I take it, is the distinguished Postmaster General, whose well known sense of justice and whose breadth of view will appeal to all of us. We regret that the parliamentary secretary, whom we all hold in high regard, has not
Supply-External Affairs authority in this matter. The Postmaster General, the distinguished leader of the house for the time being, will see the force of this argument and having the authority will I am sure accede at once to the request of the hon. member for Essex East.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The mood and temper of the house has been so pleasant tonight that I shall do nothing to upset it in any way. However there have been a number of statements made which are rather difficult for me to allow to remain uncontroverted. I shall correct them with perhaps calmer deliberation than my inclinations would lead me to venture.
I have to say to my hon. friend from Laurier that he is quite wrong in his suggestion that these final supplementaries ought to have been incorporated in earlier supplementaries. They could not have been and they should not have been, and if it were proper under our rules I could elaborate in detail to the hon. gentleman on the reasons why that is the case. May I say to him and the hon. gentleman from Bonavista-Twillingate that the only unusual item in these supplementaries, when compared with those of the last few years, is the item dealing with T.C.A.
The bulk of these final supplementary estimates are in three items, the agricultural prices support program $23.1 million, the C.N.R. deficit $67.3 million, and the T.C.A. deficit, $6.5 million, making a total of $96.9 million. The remainder of the budgetary items in these final supplementaries of $25.9 million compare most favourably with the usual governmental costs provided for in previous final supplementary estimates.
Because of what my hon. friend said I would point out that if you eliminate from the last 10 years in the final supplementary estimates those matters you ought to eliminate, the T.C.A. deficit, the C.N.R. deficit, the old age security fund deficit and the agricultural prices support costs, you will find these statistics: 1952-53, $41.8; 1953-54, $58.6; 1954-55, $47.6; 1955-56, $16.5; 1956-57, $84.8, for a total in those five years of $249.3 million. Let us take the next five years: 1957-58, $48.0; 1958-59, $32.2; 1959-60, $15.6; 1960-61, $41.2; 1961-62, $25.9, or a total of $162.9 million. In other words during the last five years of the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite the total of the final supplementaries was $249 million, and in the last five years under this government the final supplementaries totalled $162 million.
You eliminate what it suits you to eliminate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
What you eliminate, and properly eliminate, are those things which I have enumerated.

Supply-External Affairs
I eliminate nothing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend eliminates nothing and that is perhaps the reason why he is in the condition he is at the present time. The hon. gentleman spoke yesterday of an $8 million duplication, but may I say to him that there are only five items, numbers 688, 694, 701, 723 and 732, which total $1,840,561, that are in any way duplicated by the supplementaries, and it would have been impossible for those who were preparing the estimates to have put these items in the earlier supplementaries.
Now I understand it has been the practice of the house on all occasions of which I am aware-I think with one or two exceptions-that the final supplementaries have been carried with very little discussion because the policy has already been determined and it is only a matter of deciding whether there is expediency and wisdom in adding to or subtracting from the amount which had been earlier determined. With the facilities available to me and with the great skilled assistants I have here, I shall endeavour to answer any questions that may be put, but I venture to suggest that the committee would be wiser to proceed in a businesslike way with its proceedings tonight and we shall see if we cannot completely satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite.

Maybe I may be allowed to say a word since I raised this matter first at eight o'clock. I must say to the parliamentary secretary that I have watched him during the past day. I have admired his skill in having a minimum of intervention from the government side, resulting in a more ready dispatch of our business than is usually the case, particularly when the Minister of Finance himself conducts the deliberations.
But the hon. gentleman has made an exception since eight o'clock. We have now been engaged in a procedural discussion for some 40 minutes. If the request had been granted at the outset we would have made some progress on the items following those in external affairs, rather than become engaged, as we have, for almost half of tonight's sitting in a procedural wrangle.
The parliamentary secretary has spoken of previous practice. I do not agree that my hon. friend has stated this correctly. It may be that the figures which he has produced, when put in proper context, allow another interpretation altogether. However my argument does not rest on that. This surely is a unique situation. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, charged with the responsibility of speaking for Canada on vital matters involving our relationship with other


states at this critical time, will be in the house tomorrow morning. He will have returned from one of the most important international conferences held since the end of the second world war and only he, on behalf of this government, is in a position to give an authoritative account of the important dispositions made at Geneva.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no doubt he will.

My hon. friend admits this. Only in committee will we be afforded the opportunity before dissolution of exchanging views with regard to these vital matters.
If this proposal is not accepted, then what is the situation which the parliamentary secretary puts parliament in tonight? He puts parliament in this position that we will be denied having a report-
What a laugh.

-from the Department of External Affairs and the opportunity to examine that report, as it should be examined in regard to matters of fundamental importance to this nation and to the peoples of the western world. We shall be denied the opportunity to discuss such things as whether we are going to have a cessation of nuclear tests, what progress has been made in disarmament, and the relationship of Canada with neutralist states vis-a-vis the United Kingdom and the United States. These are matters of the greatest moment.
Order.
Hon. gentlemen say "order". They may not be interested in the importance of this matter, but the country is.
You will get the report tomorrow.

I say that on a matter of such vital importance parliament is being made look ridiculous tonight as a result of the decision, which is being forced on the parliamentary secretary as the spokesman of the government on this occasion. Here we have two ministers of the crown, two members of the government, who sit with the cabinet in discussing these matters.
There are five now.

That makes my argument all the stronger. Yes, the Minister of National Defence is here. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is here. He has some knowledge of these questions. I am sure he will appreciate the significance of

what I am saying. The refusal of the parliamentary secretary-undoubtedly not because of his own judgment but because of a decision imposed on him by the government- means that this parliament will not be given the procedural opportunity-
That is a lot or nonsense.
-to get from the Secretary of State for External Affairs a report on one of the most vital conferences-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

Yes, when I have finished-which has been held since the end of world war II. This puts into proper perspective the boast of the Prime Minister and the boast of others in the government of their efforts on behalf of peace. I have no doubt that this government is anxious to do something constructive in this field, but this is being denied-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then why make that insinuation?

I am making the insinuation because we are now being refused the opportunity of a discussion with regard to foreign affairs at this critical time. In view of the return tonight of the Secretary of State for External Affairs it should not be denied to a free people in a free parliament.
What is the alternative if the parliamentary secretary refuses this request, and apparently he is going to? I would point out how ridiculous this situation is, because here we have the parliamentary secretary, not to the Prime Minister but to the Minister of Finance, an amiable gentleman, an able gentleman admittedly, competent in the particular department to which he is assigned, telling us, "Do not worry; I will get up and I will give you all of the answers to these various questions" in a department that requires, if any department does, the quality of the specialist. Yet the parliamentary secretary says, "I will tell you all about Laos. I will tell you all about the discussions between Mr. Harriman and the royal Laotian government. I will tell you why Bulgaria, a communist country, supported Canada in its position against the United Kingdom and the United States in Geneva".
Who is being silly now?
And by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
And by the leader of the socialist party. If this request is not granted, what will be the consequence? The consequence will be, as I am sure the leader of that party will agree-
Who is your leader today?

-that under departmental administration we will engage in a discussion of foreign policy; that is obvious. I know that my hon. friend has on his desk three packages of speeches on foreign policy which he proposes to deliver. I have three too, and I propose to engage in such a discussion. But we are not going to make any advance this way. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs were here, these observations-
This is nonsense.
I hope that the hon. gentleman will not apply the rule of closure, because the Prime Minister has decided that we are going to eliminate closure and I am to be allowed to express myself.
This is not 1956.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am having some difficulty in hearing the hon. member for Essex East because of the interjections. I think it would be in the interest of progressing these items if the committee gave the hon. member a fair hearing, and I would ask his co-operation also in holding closely to the point of relevancy, with regard to which I am having some difficulty in reaching a decision; therefore I would ask his co-operation.
Mr. Chairman, you will have that co-operation.
Oh, oh.
I have nothing very much more to say. I have been sincere in the suggestion I have made-

No, you are not sincere.
2316	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs

-in asking that this request for postponement be granted. Let us briefly recall the context of the request, Mr. Chairman. Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs is arriving from Geneva tonight some time between the hours of ten o'clock and midnight.
How do you know?

I know because I made a point of asking his office when he was arriving, and that is what I was told. He will be in his seat tomorrow. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been at a conference that can be described as a momentous one, one involving our relations with the east, our relations with the Soviet union and our relations with countries behind the iron curtain in matters which we all admit are the most important on our agenda. All I am asking is that in view of this, the first item of departmental administration and the other items in the Department of External Affairs be postponed until tomorrow so we can have the advantage of having, in addition to the parliamentary secretary, the special knowledge and the special authority of the minister charged with these important matters.
Surely this is not an unreasonable request. To deny this request will place this government in the position, on the eve of a dissolution of parliament, of having denied this house the opportunity of discussing matters which we all regard as foremost in our considerations.
Since when?

That very junior hon. member for York-Scarborough asks, "Since when?". Obviously he has not lived long enough to realize that these problems have concerned the people of Canada for a long time and their concern is increasing.
Oh, oh.

The situation, notwithstanding these interventions and regrettable catcalls in a discussion of this kind, is that if we are denied this request let it be known that this government, which regards itself as loyal to the traditions of a free parliament-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And is.
-has taken a step to deny us, on the eve of dissolution-
How do you know?
-the opportunity of examining the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the vital matter of our foreign relations. That is the situation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is utterly ridiculous.

The parliamentary secretary has replied. I ask the ministers who are sitting behind him to speak for the government. I suppose the senior minister is the Postmaster General, and I ask him to rise in his place and tell us, is it the policy of the government of Canada in the present circumstances to deny parliament the right of hearing from the Secretary of State for External Affairs under conditions that will enable us to interrogate him?
We will hear from him.

My hon. friend says. "We will hear from him"; but what will happen tomorrow is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will come into this house and on motions he will make a statement. The Speaker, of course, will allow spokesmen for the two opposition parties to reply, but those replies will obviously be, as always, pro forma. There will be no opportunity for a serious discussion.
The consequence of this refusal is that we are going to be denied asking questions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I now appeal to the senior minister in this house, if he has the authority, to allow us to postpone this matter so that we can go on with the next item, which is the Department of Finance, a department for which the parliamentary secretary is particularly qualified to speak, and to leave the discussion of external affairs to the man who is pre-eminent in that field because of his post, and because of his experience in Geneva. The Canadian people do want a report from him and do wish to give to opposition groups the opportunity of stating their position and to elicit from the minister further information. If this request is denied, this government will stand condemned, as it deserves to be.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
It
has never been the case that a loud voice, a red face and a pompous manner will make a sound argument out of something which has no substance whatsoever. That remains as true tonight, after what we have heard, as it has been after so many other arguments put up by the hon. member over the months.
He himself, speaking at great length, has listed a number of things he would like to drag by the tail into this debate and discuss in the presence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He himself knows perfectly well, as has been ably pointed out by the parliamentary secretary, that this is not customary, that this is not in accordance with the traditions of this chamber and that it

offends all the rules, practices and traditions of this committee. Second, he has asked whether it is the policy of the government -these were the ringing terms he used-to deny freedom of discussion. It is not. We have remained here for an hour and heard the hon. member wander all over the map. He is free to remain here and waste that much time. He certainly is doing that extremely well-wasting the time of the committee and wasting the time of the entire country with his specious arguments. He is able to do that.
Tomorrow, or at some appropriate time, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will do that which is customary. He will come to this house and give on the order for motions a report at length on matters which have concerned him while he has been away. The hon. member, or more probably his leader, will have the opportunity to comment on that, as will the representative of the other group in the house. This will give an adequate opportunity to air fully all those matters which cannot be aired tonight because the secretary of state is not here.
The hon. member makes a great case out of the suggestion that there will be no further discussion possible because this parliament is going to be dissolved, apparently in a matter of hours, according to him. I do not know where he gets his information-
Maybe I am closer to the Prime Minister than is the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
But
it so happens it is not the hon. member's privilege to decide when parliament will be dissolved, and if he continues in his present vein it will never be his privilege no matter how long he lives.
I say merely in closing-and I have tried to be brief because to me the time of this committee is valuable, and the matters which we discuss here are important-
Oh.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We
are most anxious as a government to proceed expeditiously with the business before us. There are other matters to be brought forward. There are measures to be discussed. It has been pointed out in great detail the amount of time which has already been spent on these estimates and on those which have preceded them. We have seen another example tonight of delay, obstructionism, of grasping at any straw which can be found in order to continue a pointless waste of time-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. So far we have had a
Supply-External Affairs fairly objective discussion and it is unfortunate that the Postmaster General should have introduced terms which have not characterized this debate so far.
Oh.

I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it is not within our rules for an hon. member of this committee to say that another hon. member is engaged in a process of obstruction. Surely no one can be charged with obstruction if he is seeking to obtain an opportunity for the discussion of questions which are of vital interest to us all. I would ask you to request the Postmaster General to recover the calm and serenity which, on occasions, he possesses, and recognize that in making the remarks he has, he was making remarks which are unparliamentary.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: As I heard the comments of the Postmaster General it appeared to me he was using the expressions he did in broad terms without particular application to any hon. member and without even particular reference to a party in the house. I cannot find that his use of language was unparliamentary, if one might apply that term.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: shall conclude, Mr. Chairman. We will not pursue this discussion of obstructionism. The point has been made, and those who read Hansard and watch this house in operation can judge for themselves the amount of time which has been wasted.
Hear, hear. This is a sad night.
Stand up when you talk.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: They can judge the amount of time which has been wasted by unnecessary repetition, by dragging in unrelated arguments-
A sad night.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The
parliamentary secretary, in piloting these estimates through the committee in the name of the Minister of Finance does so with the complete support of the government. The position which he has taken on this matter is a sound one. It is one which is completely in keeping with the traditions and practices of this committee, and it is the position which is taken by the government itself.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
If I may intervene briefly for a moment, may I say that I am concerned about the fact that we are not dealing with the item which is before the

Supply-External Affairs committee for consideration. I am worried about the fact that we are not getting on with this discussion. I hope the hon. member for Kootenay West, to whom I shall give the floor since he rose before the hon. member for Laurier, has this in view.

I am very sorry that the parliamentary secretary, and, later, the minister, did not respond favourably to the eloquent, logical and moving appeal of the hon. member for Essex East. I think that hon. member was fully justified in saying this committee should have the opportunity to hear a full report from the Secretary of State for External Affairs before proceeding with these estimates.
I listened carefully to the arguments of the parliamentary secretary and of the minister, but it seems to me that those arguments would apply if these were just tidbits of incidentally supplementary estimates brought forward in the normal way. But we are not operating in normal circumstances or times. These are abnormal times. This house has been in session since early in January and it has not had an opportunity to discuss foreign affairs during one of the most serious periods in the world's history.
Since the plea of the hon. member for Essex East has been denied, and in the knowledge that the opposition is determined to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I think we could very profitably spend the next hour discussing a matter of great importance to the Canadian people, to the people of British Columbia and to all the people of my constituency, namely, the question of the Columbia river treaty. This is a story that should be told to the Canadian people and I am going to take advantage of the situation this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order. You have indicated before, Mr. Chairman, that you had doubts about the relevancy of the discussion which has been going on for an hour. I draw to your attention that there is nothing in this item which would allow a discussion such as has been going on up to now. The rule applicable, as you know, is the rule of strict relevancy. Furthermore, this is a matter of a further supplementary estimate. I have referred Your Honour in previous debates to May's comments at page 738 of the latest edition.
I am sure the hon. member for St. Henri will have something to contribute to this discussion because he is so knowledgeable on the rules of the house. If he cares to contribute I would be most happy to hear him, but in the meantime I suppose I have the floor and the hon. member will permit me to continue.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
I know that hon. members on the other side have previously endeavoured to prevent me from rising on points of order because of my having occupied the position which you, Mr. Chairman, now occupy. But may I remind hon. members that it is the duty of all hon. members to help the Chair to apply the rules of the House of Commons notwithstanding the fact that one may have had some experience in the chair. What the hon. members have been discussing here is entirely out of order. If they wish to do so, they may move that the item be allowed to stand. That is their business. But discussing whether we could hear the report of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the conference at Geneva would be completely outside the scope of debate which would be allowed under this estimate.
Because the hon. member for Essex East or the hon. member for Kootenay West suspects that there might be dissolution is no reason for altering the rules of the House of Commons. The house could not work on any such assumption. I therefore think that until the committee agrees to changing the rules, whatever may be the argument of hon. members with regard to dissolution, I think it is the duty of this committee to adhere to the rules.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I rise on the point of order which the minister has been discussing. I am sure Your Honour has been greatly assisted by the remarks of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys who relatively recently left the position you now hold. I am sure he is wise and well versed in the rules of the house. However, in his reference to the rule on the item under discussion with which hon. members are quite familiar, there is one thing which the minister seems to forget. That is why I chose to rise on the point of order. When there has been a discussion such as the one which has been going on today, and a statement such as the one which has been allowed on the part of the Postmaster General who I regret is absent from the house, as I have something to tell him particularly-
Mr. Pallet!: On the point of order?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -I think it is the duty of the Chair-and I say this respectfully-to allow those who wish to say something in answer to what has been said by the Postmaster General, an opportunity to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: This is not on the same point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I am speaking on the same point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am speaking on exactly the same point of order as was the minister.
The minister gave us a lecture.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; the minister who seems to have become so well versed-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I have had enough from your side.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He deserves to have some.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I have said that we have had enough lectures from your side.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If one is to judge by the conduct of the minister the other evening in his interruptions-
Order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -from that side of the house then I think-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member has referred to my conduct in other circumstances. If he wishes to deal with it I have no objection. However I hope Your Honour will allow me in turn to deal with it. Otherwise, I think the hon. member should revert to the point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: That is a question of privilege. The hon. member has referred to my conduct, and this is not relevant to the point of order which at present is being discussed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will keep his mind in peace and resume his seat I will discuss the point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister is very sensitive about points of order and questions of privilege. When he is subject to attack, he feels that he must rise. Sometimes I think he has a persecution complex.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Oh, no.
The hon. member is the one who has that. He changed ridings.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If there is a point of order, and as he rose on a point of order, I think he should at least allow me to complete the point which I had in mind to make. I was coming back to the point which I intended to raise in the first instance. What I wish to say in connection with this matter is that it is not at all accurate for the Postmaster General or the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance to state in this chamber that the rules of the House of Commons have been breached by what has been done by my
Supply-External Affairs friend the hon. member for Essex East and the rest of us who have taken part in this debate. In answer to that assertion I wish to put on Hansard what took place on March 18, 1957-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Order.
It is a point of order. You cannot have a point of order on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: .-under circumstances which were not unlike these. On March 18, 1957, as found at page 2431 of Hansard there was under discussion an item-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Stick to the point of order-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No point of order can be taken when one is already under discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I am not raising a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I am quite prepared to hear the hon. member for Laurier out. I just wish the members of the committee to reflect on this quotation from May's 16th edition at page 737 where he states as follows:
If the sum demanded by a supplementary estimate is of the same order of magnitude as the original estimate, the chairman has allowed questions of policy to be raised upon it which would have been in order if it had been an original estimate; but if the supplementary estimate is merely to provide additional funds of a relatively moderate amount required in the normal course of working of the services for which the original vote was demanded,-
These are the words which I thought hon. members ought to note.
-only the reasons for the increase can be discussed and not the policy implied in the service which must be taken to have been settled by the original vote; nor can savings be discussed.
I am sorry that I interrupted the hon. member for Laurier. However at that point the committee was experiencing a series of interruptions in any event and I just thought I should refresh the memories of hon. members of the committee with regard to that very important authority. I will now hear what the hon. member for Laurier has to say.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the chairman for having brought to my attention the matter with which he has just dealt. I think I shall be able to conclude what I have to say rather quickly. I would draw Your Honour's attention at once to the fact that these estimates have reference to $130 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Not this item.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: These items.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Not this item.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am trying to deal with what the chairman has said. If my hon. friend had

Supply-External Affairs been listening to the remarks of the Chair, he would not have made that interruption as the Chair was indicating that when one deals with the ordinary estimates, that is the rule. The point I am trying to make is that these estimates are not ordinary estimates since they are of the magnitude of $138 million, of which $67 million have to do with the deficit of the Canadian National Railways and $6.7 million have to do with-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: We are dealing with external affairs now.
Order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am now told that we are dealing with external affairs. Surely, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to be denied the opportunity of replying to the inaccurate statement made by the Postmaster General and also the parliamentary secretary. I wish to reply to that statement. The Postmaster General said that the rules of this House of Commons were not being adhered to. He said that what we were doing is not customary in a debate such as this one because it offends against all the rules of the house. That is not so. That statement is not accurate and I intend to prove that it is not accurate, I intend to do so by a reference which can be found at page 2431 of Hansard of March 18, 1957. The house was then discussing item 546, "Production service-Health of animals", the last supplementary estimate. Mr. Gardiner was in his place and was being questioned on that item. If hon. members will only take the trouble to go to Hansard they will see that for a period of two hours, from eight o'clock in the evening when the committee resumed, the committee discussed item 546 until it adjourned at ten o'clock the same night, because the hon. member for Assiniboia called it "ten o'clock" and progress was reported. There are almost 20 pages of discussion on the last supplementary estimates, so that I am surprised that the Postmaster General, who should know better because he has been in this house longer than the parliamentary secretary, should try to tell us what he did. Then there is this other statement-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: What was the total time taken on supplementary estimates in that session?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What was that again?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the Postmaster General-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There can be no point of order. The minister, who was chairman of committees of the house, should at least know what the rules are and should not be interrupting me on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Will the hon. member permit
a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When I sit down, yes, I will allow the minister to ask a question. I ask the minister to resume his seat.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I do not think the interruptions are helping us to make progress on the point of order and I think they should be modulated, if I may use that word, to permit the hon. member for Laurier to complete his point. I would remind the committee that the hon. member who had the floor before the discussion started was the member for Kootenay West and I hope we can bring this to a conclusion as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will do my best, but I assure you I would have been finished a long time ago if it had not been for these interruptions. There are just two other points and I will make them as quickly as I can. The minister has said that there has been obstruction and delay. I say to the minister and the parliamentary secretary that if there has been obstruction and delay with reference to these estimates it has been obstruction and delay on the other side of the house. On behalf of the opposition I made the offer to the house leader last week in connection with these estimates that if the Minister of Finance would tell the house what the urgent measures were that had to be dealt with and which were holding up cheques of civil servants and holding up cheques in regard to any other matters having to do with these estimates, we would consider those items and pass them at once if need be. I went a step further and said that if he wanted to include them in an appropriation bill we would be willing to pass that appropriation bill quickly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was the earlier set of supplementaries.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There has been no response to that offer and that surely is some indication of delay. The other point is that we were told we would be dealing with these estimates beginning Wednesday of this week. Under what rule of the house, either in the rules as we know them here or any change, is it the right of the government to tell us that we must dispose of these estimates within three days? That is exactly the effect of the statement made by the house leader.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon. member for Laurier has progressed into a discussion of the business of the house, to some extent in retrospect. I feel now that no ruling is really called for and I think

we should perhaps give the floor back to the hon. member for Kootenay West if that is agreeable.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I always obey your rulings, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: There should be a ruling made on the point of order I raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the Chair has forgotten what the point of order was.
I think Your Honour is very wise to forget.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: If Your Honour will permit me I will remind you that it had to do with the rule of relevancy, but as the hon. member for Laurier was permitted to revive the whole debate I understand, of course, that Your Honour might have forgotten what the point of order was.

Mr. Chairman, with your permission I should like to take advantage of the time available to discuss a matter of great concern to the Canadian people, particularly the people of British Columbia and more particularly the constituents I have the honour to represent, namely, the Columbia river treaty. I think we are justified in doing so under the rules because during recent weeks and months we had read of discussions and differences between the federal government and the government of British Columbia. Members of this house are quite uncertain as to the direction in which matters are proceeding.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-
Surely you are not going to interfere. Surely members of this house have some rights.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon.
member spoke for about half an hour and he should give someone else a chance to say something.
Closure. Totalitarianism.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Surely we are as much entitled to raise a point of order as the hon. member. The point I should like to make, Mr. Chairman, is that your predecessor in the chair a few moments ago read a citation from May, page 738, which said that if the amount of the estimate to be considered is comparatively small-I do not know what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would say about that; I think I overheard him say it was three or four million dollars-

For external affairs, $4 million.
Supply-External Affairs

The total amount of these estimates for 1961-62 is $93 million and the proportion is three or four million dollars to $93 million. Would the chairman think that would justify embarking upon a discussion of the Columbia river project at this stage of the supplementary estimates or should the hon. member not be confined to asking questions regarding the various items that are to be considered tonight? There is an item of $225,000 for departmental administration. Surely that does not justify hon. members embarking upon all sorts of questions having to do with policy.
Does the hon. member not think $4 million is a lot of money?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is a great deal of money in my books.
You belittled it. "What's $4 million", you said.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I did not
say that.

We do not
have a Mr. Howe over here.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am referring to what is said in May.

I should like to say a word on the point of order that the distinguished Solicitor General has raised. It is true that the item for departmental administration is only $225,000 but an extra $4 million is being asked for the Department of External Affairs in these supplementary estimates-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Why don't you discuss it then?

-which is a very considerable fraction of the total amount voted for this department. It seems to me that it is not an insignificant amount in the eyes of the Canadian people, however insignificant it may seem to the Solicitor General and to the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary. Moreover, even $225,000 is the cost of restoring Arizona Charlie's and that is a large amount of money.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the point of order, I would call on the hon. member for Kootenay West and I will listen to what he has to say. If he gets too far from the realm of relevancy I will be able to remind him.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I will stay strictly within a subject that comes under the administration of the Department of External Affairs. Let me say to the Solicitor General, who used his best efforts to try to stop me speaking for my constituents, that not only am I speaking for the party I have the honour to represent

Supply-External Affairs but I am also speaking for a large number of people who support his party and a large number who support the Liberal party who have asked me to take the first opportunity available in the house to place before it certain information with respect to this development from the local point of view and certain information with respect to the engineering aspects of the Columbia river treaty. If I am denied this opportunity now I will have to go home and say that I had closure applied to me by a member of the cabinet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, no one seeks to apply closure to anyone. We only seek to have the rules of the house applied fairly and equally to all members of the committee. In the particular departmental administration item now before the committee there is nothing which relates to the Columbia river treaty. Anything that relates to the Columbia river treaty will be found in the administration item of the main estimates under international joint commission. There is not a dollar in this item, I suggest to the hon. gentleman, who is one of our most experienced and genial parliamentarians and who at least should set an example to the house as to how we in this house should conduct ourselves, for this Columbia river. The hon. member should be an example rather than treating the house to the farce to which we have been treated tonight by that distinguished hon. member for Essex East.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to speak to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to deal with the outburst and loss of temper-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Oh no, I just enjoyed myself.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -which is not often displayed by the hon. member.
He is getting more like the Minister of Finance all the time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As my hon. friend from Bona-vista-Twillingate says, he is imitating the Minister of Finance a great deal. The point my friend makes is not well taken. I submit that under the item for departmental administration it is the privilege of hon. members to deal with any part of matters having to do with the department. This is what I tried to show earlier when I put on the record, before Your Honour was in the chair, what happened under similar circumstances with the item concerning the Department of Agriculture. From eight o'clock until ten a discussion took place and the item was not passed until then. I say, therefore, with respect that the parliamentary secretary is


entirely wrong in what he says. We have an item headed, departmental administration, and even though there is nothing in it having to do with the international joint commission, the Columbia river project is not a matter that concerns exclusively the international joint commission. Surely my friend will concede that. Under those circumstances I say to you, with respect, that the hon. member for Kootenay West has the right to do what he was doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I point out to Your Honour that I cited to the deputy chairman of committees, when this point was first raised, the rule that is laid down in May's last edition. It is on page 738 and is to the effect that a general policy debate is not allowed under an item such as this. May I suggest to Your Honour that the rules of the house do not belong only to the opposition but to the whole house. When there is obstruction every member, those on the government side and in the opposition, suffer from it. All members suffer when the rules are not adhered to by members on all sides.

I should like to say a word precisely on the point that has been raised. I referred earlier to what happened during the consideration of the last supplementary estimates brought before this house by a government that respected the rights of hon. members in committee of supply. During the consideration of an item for citizenship and immigration, because there had been new developments, because the Hungarian business had come up since the regular estimates had been passed, the government of that day, knowing the facts of the situation and the fact that this was a national forum, allowed discussion of the matter without points of order being raised. Another matter in which hon. gentlemen were greatly interested at that time was George Christian Hanna, who had come in at that time, and the present Prime Minister was making great humanitarian speeches about him, the same Prime Minister who later deported him. These subjects were discussed at great length without any points of order being raised, without any attempt by Mr. Harris or anyone else on the front benches to stifle debate in the way it is being stifled by these incessant points of order from these hon. gentlemen opposite.
We would have had half of these estimates through this evening if the reasonable request of the hon. member for Essex East had been met. Probably all the estimates would have been through, except external affairs, if hon. members opposite had not dug in their heels and stubbornly refused to have the minister

here when he could be here tomorrow. This is the minister whose estimates we are being asked to pass.
We have not taken any objection to the fact the Minister of Finance is not here. We remember one evening when Mr. Drew was leader of the opposition and he refused to proceed with the estimates because they were being piloted by a parliamentary secretary without the minister being in the chamber. He made a terrific scene about it. It seems to me we have shown some courtesy to the parliamentary secretary in not raising this point that the Minister of Finance is not here. When we say that the minister whose estimates are being considered ought to be here and make a reasonable request that they be held up until he gets here, this request is refused. We are accused of obstruction. It is a pretty topsy-turvy kind of attitude to the rules and to the practices of parliament being exhibited by hon. gentlemen opposite.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think
it is an unreasonable request to have an opportunity to discuss this subject because it has been a fluid situation. There have been differences of opinion since we last discussed the subject between the federal and provincial governments; there have been differences of opinion between ministers of the crown and ministers in the United States. The Prime Minister and the ministers of the government have answered questions directed to them to try to elicit information. Surely, Mr. Chairman, one should have an opportunity of presenting the views of one's constituents which are broadly based and broadly held.
Now, Mr. Chairman, if I could be allowed to proceed-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I listened with great interest to the general remarks the hon. member has just made. I think I should caution him before he goes into detail on the subject that he should keep his remarks in rather general terms. As the parliamentary secretary has pointed out, there is no money being requested in this group of supplementary estimates for the subject on which the hon. member has embarked. On the other hand, we have a vote concerning administration. Even in May there are citations restricting debate and other citations which seem to enlarge it a bit. While remembering the rule of relevancy and also that the Columbia river development is not mentioned in the item, I will permit the hon. member to make a few general remarks. However, if he gets into particulars about the subject, I think then he will definitely be transgressing the leniency the Chair is supposed to allow.
Supply-External Affairs

You impose a very particular burden on me, Mr. Chairman, to talk in general terms about the particular or, in other words, to talk in abstract terms about the concrete. I shall do the best I can. I think what I am going to say, Mr. Chairman, will be of interest to members because this is a matter of some substance. I wanted to tell members, first, of the particular local details in connection with this matter. I am quite sure that under these estimates there is some provision for entertainment related to the Columbia project. If you look at one or two of the items, I think they could be related to the Columbia river treaty. There would be certain hospitality extended when these gentlemen come up from the United States.
You mean the Minister of Finance entertained them?

I am speaking of the Department of External Affairs. I am sure they would not allow Mr. Udall to come to Canada without treating him to a nice dinner or refreshments. I think in that way I can relate the item to the Columbia river treaty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As someone remarked on a previous occasion, that would be really taxing the imagination of the chairman to accept such a viewpoint. Unless the hon. member can state it in a more specific way than he has done, I cannot see that this estimate for $225,000 could relate by near or by far to the Columbia river. I know the difficulty of the hon. member, but still these difficulties spring not from the ruling of the Chair but from the rules as they were made, and these must be applied. I think the hon. member will have to base his discussion within the limits involved.

There is another item here, representation abroad, operational expenses, travelling expenses, postage, telephones and telegrams. Could you assure me that none of that money is to be spent on telephone calls or telegrams in connection with this matter?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is on a different item. He has gone on to the next item. Right now we are on item No. 692.
But it comes under "departmental administration."

Could I ask the chairman if the Chair and the hon. members of the house realize the consequences of the disposition that is being made of this matter? The contention is made that because under the departmental estimate no particular expenditure is proposed, then that precludes a discussion of this particular matter. When the original item is proposed or when, as

Supply-External Affairs is now the case, we are discussing further items of proposed expenditure under departmental administration, surely that ruling in May does not mean what the minister of mines suggests? Surely under our procedures, under departmental administration it is open to us to discuss anything having to do with administration, whether it involves expenditure or not. That is the rule; and to interpret May as is suggested by the Deputy Speaker is, I believe, stretching the rule. Also, while I am speaking, I would suggest to you that there are not many precedents in this house when former presiding officers have chosen to influence the course of procedural decisions as we have had it done tonight.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair would very much like to be enlightened if the hon. member had a precise citation.
Well, it is common sense.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member had a precise citation covering this matter I would certainly like to hear it, but in the absence of such a precise citation I can only go by rule 59, paragraph 2-
Which does not say that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -which says the discussion must be relevant-
Of course.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -and I must also bring forward the principles that are enunciated at page 738 of May. I have not stopped the hon. member yet. I have only cautioned him to remain within this scope. I appreciate his difficulty. I think he is trying to co-operate with the Chair and perhaps we should allow him to continue.

On a point of order. I asked while Your Honour was talking, if I could see May's book. I suggest on reading his citation it does not lend itself to the interpretation which Your Honour has put on it. It says "relevant," but what the hon. gentleman is discussing is a matter which comes under the administration of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and to say he is precluded from discussing a matter under this item, which does not at this particular time involve a proposed expenditure, is stretching the meaning of the citation beyond reasonable terms. That is what I am saying.
I am not offering any citation. I am simply asking for a literal interpretation of what the English language says in May.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As interpreted by Martin's bureau of statistics.
IMr. Martin (Essex East).]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That is what the Chair is trying to do. The deputy chairman read from May a little time before I took the chair, and there are certain lines which are particularly applicable to the present case. For instance:
As a general rule, on the supplementary estimates it is in order to discuss only the particular items which constitute the supplementary estimates and the sub-heads of the original estimates can only be referred to so far as they are involved in the fair discussion of the points contained in the items asked for in the supplementary estimates. Of course, it is quite obvious that it should be improper, as a general rule, to raise on a supplementary estimate the whole question of policy involved in the original estimate-
That is right.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Further down it says:
-if the supplementary estimate is merely to provide additional funds of a relatively moderate amount required in the normal course of working of the services for which the original vote was demanded, only the reasons for the increase can be discussed and not the policy implied in the service which must be taken to have been settled by the original vote.
I believe that the general gist of all of that is that under the main estimate of administration, as everyone knows here, all phases of departmental administration and all matters affecting the department can be discussed; but here we are limited by the fact that we are only asked for certain additional sums and we are further limited in our discussion by the details of that estimate. Unless the hon. member can relate his remarks to these sub-heads I cannot really see how he would be in order.

I think I can do that very easily. I notice that $33,000 of this particular additional amount-as the hon. member for Kootenay West directed our attention to it -is for telephones, telegrams and other communication services. Only three days ago the Prime Minister admitted in this house that he had received a message on this very subject from the government of the United States, and no one will make me believe- unless the minister produces all his messages and shows it is not true-that no part of this $33,000 is not being used for communications with regard to the Columbia which no longer, contrary to what the parliamentary secretary has indicated, has to do with the I.J.C. This is a treaty, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs is responsible for the decision as to whether or not that treaty will be brought before the house and whether it will be ratified. So, it is entirely within departmental administration, and there is in this item a detail which prima facie has to do with the Columbia. Probably a great part of this $33,000 had to be used because of the difficulty over the Columbia.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I thank the hon. member tor his valuable contribution and I am convinced that the hon. member for Kootenay West would be in order if he asked the parliamentary secretary whether any sums of money being asked were applied to phone calls made in regard to this matter; but he is not entitled, as far as I can see, to discuss the general matters of the Columbia river development.

Well, Mr. Chairman, this is an unusual circumstance and there have been continuing and changing developments with respect to this matter. This is an entirely new matter arising out of the circumstances of the signing of this treaty. I wanted to give this information to the house because I was asked to give it at the first opportunity. So far as the provincial government is concerned, and I say this without any hesitation, in my opinion it has acted in bad faith in this matter. I agree with what the federal government did so far as the treaty is concerned, not its effect, terms and details, but I do think that the provincial government has acted in bad faith in leading this government to believe it agreed with the terms of the treaty, whether directly or indirectly, permitting this government to sign it, and then changing its course of conduct shortly afterwards. I think that should let me off the hook. Anyway, the provincial government held hearings which were conducted by the water controller.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How the provincial government comes into this is surely something the hon. gentleman has not explained to the committee in any way.
What is parliament being reduced to?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is the hon. gentleman who is endeavouring to reduce parliament to something by his exaggerated histrionics and by the buffoonish contortionism he is conducting tonight.

All I can say to
the parliamentary secretary is that what he is trying to do is prevent us from talking, depriving us of the right to free discussion in this house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the most utter nonsense the hon. gentleman has ever uttered in this house, and he is a past master at uttering nonsense in the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think anybody is trying to stifle anybody else. As far as the Chair is concerned-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not so sure.
Supply-External Affairs

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -it is only interested in promoting free and uninhibited discussion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can we hear from the Minister of Justice?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
But the Chair is fettered by the rules, which all hon. members of the committee have freely accepted. I know that the hon. member for Kootenay West, who is a great expert on the conduct of this house, will want to abide by the rules to which he was a party.
I am forced to agree with the parliamentary secretary that in introducing affairs concerning the provincial government the hon. member was getting out of order. Although he is committed to raising this matter at the first opportunity, I do not believe that this is the right opportunity to do so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, do you really agree with the conduct of the parliamentary secretary?
Sit down.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He almost crossed the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was not discussing any hon. member's conduct; I was only discussing the ideas expressed, and I mentioned one aspect of his remarks with which I had to agree. I am sure the hon. member who has the floor will abide by the rules.

I wonder if I might make an appeal to Your Honour. On Monday of this week the Prime Minister came in here and asked the house in a very conciliatory way to join him in an effort to abolish the closure rule. Could we not proceed, sir, in the spirit in which the Prime Minister began the activities of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is what we are asking you to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure we were all inspired by those motives, but this is not a discussion about closure.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, I don't know, sir.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As a matter of fact the rules exist as they are to prevent closure and to permit free debate. If it were open to every hon. member to introduce any subject that came into his head upon every item, obviously no business would be transacted at all. The only purpose of the rules is that the business shall be transacted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No, we will be here for days at this rate.

Mr. Chairman, I was going to mention the hearings held by the water

Supply-External Affairs controller as part of his responsibility under provincial law in connection with this treaty. He held hearings at Kaslo, Revelstoke, Na-kusp and Castlegar and over 1,000 people attended those hearings. Three hundred people made written or verbal representations before the controller. I want to bring this to the attention of the ministers concerned because it was one of the most unusual circumstances in Canadian history. Here, in connection with this treaty, is a water controller acting in a judicial capacity to make a decision as to whether a licence would be given, while at the same time the water controller was part of the British Columbia negotiating team representing British Columbia and pressing for the building of the High Arrow and other dams. He was praised by the minister of lands and forests in the province of British Columbia for his work in promoting it alongside his pal Dr. Keenleyside. Then at the same time he signs a report of the British Columbia energy board in which the same subject is discussed and the same matter is dealt with. I raised this point first of all-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I suggest that you have an interpreter for the hon. member for Kootenay West, because apparently he does not understand your ruling.
Oh, such insolence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Order.
A junior member of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure that the hon. member did understand my ruling.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He does not abide by it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think he has adhered strictly to it. In introducing matters in connection with provincial bodies I am not quite sure whether he is even on external affairs; in any event he is certainly not on item 692. I would ask the hon. member's co-operation, because after all there are quite a number of items here and there are probably many hon. members who wish to speak on this particular item and have relevant contributions to make. I hope the hon. member's contributions will likewise be relevant.
I will try and make them relevant, Mr. Chairman, by saying that the people who attended these hearings have asked me to rise in this house and repeat briefly what was said at those hearings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Do it at the right time.
They wish me to mention briefly some of the things that were said at those hearings.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Irrelevancy.
I am speaking to the government of the day on behalf of my constituents and organizations in my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Do it at the right time.

I must explain, Mr. Chairman, that they protest most vigorously that here a treaty was signed without any survey being made of the land which was being flooded, or of its value, without any proper estimate of the cost of the public facilities that were to be flooded-over 20 docks and wharves, and things of that sort-and with no estimate as to the destruction of the forest industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman.
For these reasons I have been asked-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The parliamentary secretary has risen on a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the rule has been specified a number of times this evening. I refer to the rule of relevancy in debate. With regard to this matter Your Honour has expressed very clearly that adherence to the rule provides for the expedition of the business of the house. I think the hon. member for Kootenay West is out of order in his remarks. I also think that the conduct of the official opposition this evening has indicated-
Order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Order. Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I agree that the parliamentary secretary was going beyond the point that the point of order warranted. However, the first part of his remarks were well taken, and again I must caution the hon. member to restrict his remarks to the item under consideration.
Mr. Chairman-
Such frivolity.
