Mr. Chairman, I am dealing in a concrete way with a problem that is related to the administration of the Department of External Affairs. I say also that there was no assessment of the damage done to the forest industry or to the fishing industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I claim that the hon. member for Kootenay West is completely defying your ruling as to relevancy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Where is the point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not believe that the hon. member is animated by a spirit of defiance, but he seems to have some difficulty in restricting his remarks to the item under consideration. Perhaps, as I tried to suggest a little earlier, this may not be the proper opportunity for the hon. member to raise the very interesting points that he wishes to raise, and perhaps he will contain his remarks until a more appropriate occasion.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, I did not clearly understand the point of order raised by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I wonder whether he would explain it to the committee once again.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, I would be very glad to do so. It was simply that the hon. member for Kootenay West was not following the instructions as to relevancy laid down by the chairman.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is that a point of order?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I would think it should be.
Mr. Chairman, on the point of order raised by the Minister of National Health and Welfare it does seem to me that he has insulted Your Honour and he has insulted the committee-
Oh, oh.

-by suggesting that Your Honour presumes to instruct any hon. member in a free parliament. I suggest that the person who needs instruction in free assemblies is the Minister of National Health and Welfare himself and that he should not be permitted to make these irrelevant interventions in a serious debate about the administration of the Department of External Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: You should not either.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: To put the hon. member's mind at ease, I must say that I was not at all incensed by what the minister said-
Your Honour should be.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
-because I feel that he said it in a spirit of co-operation to try and expedite the business of the committee. Perhaps the same spirit of co-operation will animate the hon. member for Kootenay West and he will now embark upon the item under discussion.
Supply-External Affairs
Mr. Chairman, would I be in order in directing a number of questions to the parliamentary secretary with a view to getting answers?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may direct his questions to the parliamentary secretary and as they arise I will decide whether or not they are relevant.

I want to know from the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance why a treaty was signed and an estimate given for a certain dam without any estimate of the cost of putting the logs of the Selgar Corporation over the dam. Does the Minister of Finance know that it will take $25 million to put the machinery in to take the logs over the dam and that the estimate in the original treaty was $50,000? Does the minister know that? Can he give me an answer?
How does the hon. member for Kootenay West arrive at that figure?
Perhaps the Minister of Justice could reply, since he has been so successful in these negotiations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would be glad to answer any questions relative to the item which is now before the committee. When this committee is dealing with this particular matter raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West I am sure he will get all the information he desires. However, the inference contained in the question asked by the hon. gentleman is erroneous. I think it comes from one man, and one man only.
Can the minister tell me if any officials of the Department of External Affairs have been informed by any official of the Selgar Corporation as to the cost of the construction of this equipment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is not a capital item, and the hon. gentleman by repeating the same question is not going to make an irrelevant question more relevant.
Surely, an official of that corporation visited the Department of External Affairs and gave the officials that information and asked for an answer.
Still not relevant.
Can the parliamentary secretary answer that question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Supply-External Affairs
When I hear the parliamentary secretary say that an underestimate of $25 million on one dam is an irrelevant question, I think I have the right to continue this debate until we get the facts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member is confusing the committee in mentioning this contract for $25 million because the vote before us is only for $225,000. The hon. member is referring to items which are foreign to the subject properly under discussion.

My point is that this is a matter which comes directly under the administration of the Department of External Affairs, and it is a matter upon which the department has been informed by this gentleman since we last had an opportunity to discuss these estimates.
Who gave you the information.
I am referring to personal conversations with a number of people who know what they are talking about.
I want to pursue the inquiry which was raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West. We know where this matter stands. This treaty has not been ratified.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What treaty?
The Columbia treaty. The government has not even dared to bring it before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How does it arise under this item?
Perhaps the Minister of Justice could reply when I have finished.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: On a point of order.
More closure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The minister of mines is rising on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knows very well that Your Honour has ruled the discussion of this matter of the Columbia treaty to be irrelevant. If I rise on a point of order it is because I feel that the worst kind of closure is the one which has been conducted by members of the opposition.

On the point of order which has been raised by a gentleman who
had an opportunity to learn something of the rules, an opportunity not given to many of us, but of which he does not seem to have made very good use, let me say it has not been ruled that any discussion of the treaty is irrelevant. Your Honour has said it is not irrelevant to discuss it in a general way.
Further, I was proceeding to demonstrate that this matter was peculiarly within the item of departmental administration because it had not been resolved. There is no capital item. There is a project. A treaty has been signed but it has not been brought before the house. It lacks ratification. We want to find out why this has not been done, why there has been this delay on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in getting on with the job. We should like to find that out from the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: On a point of order-
Surely not another of those dreadful points of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I had risen on a point of order but I wish to withdraw it because it is ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is asking for information it is the first time there has been any real request for information from across the floor tonight. The opposition has been interested in wrangling, bickering and squabbling, not in a constructive request for information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I really regret to have to interrupt this debate at this time, but the clock indicates that it is ten o'clock and it is therefore my duty to ask the committee if I may rise, report certain resolutions and request leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house.
Item stands.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
